# THE TRANSLATOR
## The Commentator <note>Original: "Scholiaste." A commentator who provides explanatory notes or "scholia" on a text.</note> to his friend, wishes all prosperity.

I do not place myself under your wings, nor do I call upon you to take up the shield for defense, nor the sword for offense; crows and dogs are permitted to croak and bark. The <term>blowers</term> <note>From the French "souffleurs," a derogatory term for amateur or fraudulent alchemists who spent their time blowing on bellows to heat their furnaces without understanding the science.</note>, charcoal-burners, deceivers, charlatans, sellers of smoke <note>A common idiom for those who sell empty promises or fraudulent secrets.</note>, sellers of recipes, of white and red powders <note>Likely referring to cosmetic pigments or perhaps the "white" and "red" stages of the alchemical Great Work.</note>, hawks <note>A "tiercelet" is a male hawk, used here to describe predatory swindlers or intermediaries.</note>, usurers of one hundred percent and fifty percent, extractors of mercury from metals, forgers of various vessels and furnaces, builders of gallows, scaffolds, and similar infamous places where these scoundrels entangle themselves after having deceived themselves and many others—they may spout off to their heart’s content. "Great is Diana of the Ephesians!" <note>A reference to the Book of Acts 19:28, signifying a crowd blindly defending their own profitable superstitions or crafts.</note> This book will describe for us, reveal to us, and take away from us...

<summary>In this preface, the translator (acting as a commentator) addresses a friend, distancing himself from the fraudulent "blowers" and swindlers who populate the fringes of alchemical practice. He positions the following text as a revelation of truth that will expose these charlatans.</summary>

# TO THE READER.

If you are as much a friend of truth as I am an enemy of falsehood, you will be a diligent student of the good authors who treat our Philosophy, the goal of which is to possess the stone commonly called **philosophical** <note>The "Philosopher’s Stone," the legendary substance sought by alchemists to transmute base metals into gold and achieve physical and spiritual perfection.</note>. You must flee from the company and conversation of all charlatans, wanderers, <term>blowers</term> <note>Original: "souffleurs." A derogatory term for "puffers"—amateurs who focused solely on the physical heat of the furnace and bellows without understanding the underlying theory.</note>, makers and sellers of recipes, extractors of <term>quicksilver</term> <note>Original: "argent vif," meaning mercury.</note>, congealers, fixers, dyers, <term>fleecers</term> <note>Original: "tire-poils," literally "hair-pullers," a term for swindlers who fleece the gullible.</note>, and similar deceivers and forgers. By duping those who are too credulous, they lead them to nothing but the noose, shame, or a miserable life. If you believe me, you will do well; otherwise, regret shall follow you.

Now, through the seventeen chapters that follow (through which I could have produced a massive volume, but chose not to in order to avoid overwhelming you), you will learn from the First: that despite the diversity of names, the <term>matter</term> <note>The "Prima Materia" or First Matter. Alchemical texts often used hundreds of different names (like "Green Lion" or "Adamic Earth") to describe a single starting substance, confusing the uninitiated.</note> is not diverse, and that it is named either for its accidental or its essential form. By the Se-

<summary>In this preface, the author warns the reader to avoid fraudulent alchemists and "puffers," promising instead a concise seventeen-chapter guide to the true "matter" of the Philosopher's Stone.</summary>
<keywords>Philosophy, philosopher's stone, charlatans, blowers, quicksilver, mercury, prima materia, alchemy, swindlers</keywords>

...ly, for there is nothing hidden, nor anything more to be desired; it is true that the **extraction** and **dissolution**, or the **nourishment of the black** <note>The "nourishment of the black" refers to the *nigredo* stage, the first phase of the alchemical Great Work, where the matter is decomposed and purified.</note> are two operations which require visual observation of the process. However, if you read this entire discourse attentively, and reread it with meditation, you will be able to achieve it; these two points are easy to do for one who understands them, yet very difficult, even for the most experienced. 

And if God grants you the grace to find them, the rest is as nothing, so to speak. Praise Him then and thank Him, and let your joy be internal; whether in working or in enjoying your harvest, be secretive, and use it for the honor and praise of Him who will have opened your eyes and sharpened your understanding, and for the consolation of the poor members of **Jesus Christ**, who must judge us all at His **second coming**, which shall occur, however long it may be delayed, at the time determined since the foundation of the world.

This, Reader, is what I wanted to tell you.

One should have a great abundance of books, and let no one persuade himself that a single book can be found which truly describes the whole art in a continuous discourse, as many foolish people believe. *Theobald van Hoghelande, page 11.*

You should not waste your goods, because (if you are not ignorant of the principles of the art) you will reach the completion of the mastery at a low price. *Geber, Book 1, Chapter 7.* <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath and foundational figure in alchemy.</note>

Hold this firmly: that for all the chapters of this most precious art, the cost of the medicines themselves does not exceed fifty silver pieces, counting from the first operation. *Arnaldus de Villa Nova, Book 2, Chapter 7 of the Rosary.* <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311) was a Catalan physician and reputed alchemist.</note>

It is necessary to bring many arguments against firmly held opinions if one wishes to lead a listener away from a previous sentiment and convert them, so that they may have faith in one’s words. Indeed, I would not have produced these [arguments] to confirm my discourse unless there were many men who opposed my opinion. *Hippocrates, Book 4 on Diseases, Section 1.*

Note that in the book of the antiquities of Paris, on page eleven, it is remarked that in the Reliquary of Saint Genevieve there are nine-score thirteen <note>193</note> and a half marks of silver at forty-five Parisian sous per mark, and eight and a half marks of gold at sixteen francs per mark; this was in the year one thousand two hundred forty-two.

And that during the reign of Louis XI in 1475, the gold *écus* <note>crowns</note> were only worth 24 Parisian sous and 6 deniers; let him who has ears and judgment understand and judge.

# CHAPTER I.

<meta>ink stains on right margin and bottom; catchword "ferme-" visible at bottom right; bleed-through from reverse page</meta>

is contrary.

This subtle, spiritual matter named "vile," having been sublimated and named *Serpent*, must be calcined <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to a high temperature to reduce it to a powder; in alchemy, this is often seen as the "death" of the material's old form</term>—that is to say, made white—by the method we will describe in its proper place; and then it is named *salt*, not because it is salty, but because it is stable, firm, and fixed, and because it can serve as an ornament to metals inferior to silver, just as salt gives grace and taste to the substances to which it is applied.

This *dissolved* matter—that is to say, extended far and wide in both quantity and quality—is named *Water* and *found everywhere*. I well know that some understand this "found everywhere" to be said because of the four Elements <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water—the fundamental building blocks of the universe in pre-modern science.</note>, which I do not contradict, but I say that this way of speaking, like many others, is used to hide the secret from the ignorant, some of whom believe it to be dew-water, urine, saltpeter, *aqua fortis* <note>original: "eau forte," a strong nitric acid used to dissolve metals</note>, *aqua regia* <note>original: "eau royale," a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids capable of dissolving gold</note>, and other waters that wet everything they are placed upon. Let it be noted, then, for the second time, that our Author does not simply say it *is* Water, but it is *named* Water and *found everywhere*. This matter, then, after being calcined, must be reduced into *oil*, and then it is called a *viscous thing* and *found in all places for sale*. One must not believe that it is a flowing, greasy, and burning oil; rather, after this matter is whitened and named Water, it is fit for whitening, but it must be made capable of remaining upon the matter onto which it will be cast, just as oil clings firmly to the piece upon which it has fallen.

Consequently, it could not be raised to redness, as he adds next, saying: having raised it to redness, it is called fire, and by the name, *of all redness*. This is not to say that it is the animal so named, for this animal (nor any other, though some say the contrary) is not conceived, nourished, and perfected in the fire; rather, this amalgam, when placed in a suitable fire, engenders therein a "son" who, through the continuation of that fire, is nourished and perfected. # CHAPTER I.

...being made water: now this water is understood in three ways: either when the whole compound is liquid, or when it is an impalpable and black powder, or when it has acquired whiteness; in all of which it is partly volatile <term>volatile: a substance that easily evaporates or escapes when heated</term>, and partly vitrifying <term>vitrifying: the process of turning into glass, or becoming "fixed" so it no longer evaporates</term>. I say and affirm it to be volatile in the black, the white, the yellow, and the red stages, being unable to be fixed upon the fire, except by its mother in the white stage, and by its father in the red stage. <margin><insert>Read</insert></margin> For the yellow is the end of the white and the beginning of the red; this is why he adds that this brass <note>original: *airain* — a term often used in alchemy to describe the base matter as it begins to transform</note> *always thickens while cooking* through the intended order, which will raise it to a most eminent degree, but one more excellent than those "Most Eminents" <note>The author likely refers to high-ranking officials or cardinals, noting that the Stone’s "splendor" is superior because it can be shared without being lost.</note> who cannot communicate their splendor to others without diminishing their own. But this brass, by communicating its most eminent purple <note>The "purple" or "red" stage is the final, most perfect state of the alchemical work.</note> to its inferiors, makes itself even more desirable, more sought after, and more admirable in all things; so that, being at such a high degree of perfection from which it can never fall, it acquires the name **Philosophers' Stone**, or the Stone of the Wise. If one calls it *water* at that point, one speaks the truth (by its properties); if one says the opposite, one does not lie (by similarity), charitably warning the reader not to get stuck on the diversity of names, so as not to be deceived.

Now, he says, *when they are cooked wisely, they become one.* They are therefore several, at least three, of which two will never agree—since one is hot and dry and the other cold and moist—except by the means and mediation of a third, a friend to both, who can unite and bind them in such a way that they will forever be inseparably *one*.

...middle, and end has a thousand names, explaining the reason for a portion of them, and leaving the other portion for the students to research.

Almost all researchers in this study strain <note>original: *alambiquent* — literally "to distill," but here used metaphorically to mean over-complicating or over-working the mind, a pun on the alchemist's alembic</note> their minds to distill, decompose, and reduce—or so they say—their materials into four simple elements, of which they claim everything is composed. Then, from such rejoined simple elements, they expect to perform miracles. But these "miracles" are the opposite of God, who from nothing—that is to say, from no visible or palpable matter—made everything that is both visible and palpable. Instead, these coarse seekers make nothing out of everything. In doing so, they fulfill the misunderstood saying of the **Philo-chemists** <note>original: *Philochymiques* — literally "lovers of alchemy," referring to the master philosophers of the craft</note> who command us to reduce the substance from which the necessary matter is drawn into its "first being." By this, they mean the nearest state and not a distant one, which is the **simple matter** that proceeds **from the dissolved body**. 

This dissolution, or annihilation, is very poorly understood by these coarse operators. This dissolution is the true **squaring of the circle** <note>a classic alchemical symbol for the union of opposites and the transformation of the physical (the square) into the spiritual (the circle)</note> reduced to the triangle, to the line, and to the indivisible point. This point contains as much in its indivisibility as did the line, the triangle, the quadrangle, and the circle, without the manual separation of any thing, but only through the attraction of new qualities, one after the other. This circle is a perfect thing to which neither nature nor man can add or subtract; only the one who is wise and learned in this science (I say science, for it is sought and desired for its own sake) knows how to lead it to a degree in which he will show more plainly...

<term>alambiquer</term> — To distill; used here to describe over-complicating the mind. 
<term>four elements</term> — Fire, Air, Water, and Earth; the traditional building blocks of matter.
<term>Philo-chemists</term> — Ancient and medieval masters of alchemical philosophy.
<term>simple matter</term> — The purified, essential substance of the Work.
<term>dissolved body</term> — Matter that has been broken down to its primary state.
<term>squaring of the circle</term> — A symbolic mathematical operation representing the completion of the Great Work.
<term>triangle</term> — Often representing the three principles: Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury.
<term>quadrangle</term> — Representing the four elements.
<term>attraction</term> — The process by which matter draws in new spiritual or physical qualities.

### CHAPTER I.

After eight days of cooking, once everything had cooled, it was poured into a vessel: truly, the said filed silver was found to weigh exactly its original weight, and the cinnabar <term>cinnabar: a bright red mineral consisting of mercury sulfide, often used in attempts to create "philosophical" mercury</term> increased in weight by about twenty ounces, so much so that this "great expert," looking at me, said, "Well now, what do you say?" Then, without answering him, I asked the Goldsmith if he wished to buy this silver that he himself had filed. To which he replied, "It is true that I filed it, but when I filed it, it was white, and now it is very black; nonetheless, I will buy it once it has been melted." Having done this on the spot and cast it into an ingot, he found his ingot diminished by about twenty-two ounces from its original weight, and very low on the touchstone <term>touchstone: a small tablet of dark stone used to test the purity of gold and silver by the color of the streak they leave when rubbed upon it</term>. And having melted the cinnabar that was said to have increased by twenty ounces in weight, it was found that the whole weighed only about nine ounces; and if the whole had been put to the cupel <term>cupel: a shallow, porous bowl used in assaying to separate precious metals from base metals by heating</term>, the loss would have been much greater. Thus was this "great Doctor" confounded by the proof, so that the cinnabar, the vessel, and the charcoal were all lost, and the silver diminished in both value and weight—of which Trevisan <note>Bernard of Treviso (1406–1490), an Italian alchemist whose writings warned against common chemical errors</note> had already given warning in his *Opuscule* <note>original: *Opuscule*; refers to a "Little Work" or short treatise</note> when speaking of the "nails of cinnabar" <note>likely a reference to a specific fraudulent alchemical process or "fixation" attempted by chemists in Paris</note> that were made in Paris.

### Scholium.

If one places a measure of water upon an equal measure of ashes, the ashes will arrest the fluidity of the water through their dryness <term>dryness: (siccité) one of the four primary qualities in ancient physics; here it acts as a stabilizing force</term>. This is what Trevisan tells us here, calling the earth the *body and bones of it*, which prevents the quicksilver <term>quicksilver: (vif argent) another name for mercury</term>, mercury, and other chemical elements from flowing—not only upon a flat surface, but even during ordinary tests; that is to say, from escaping either during simple melting or in the cupel <term>cupel: a porous vessel used in refining to separate precious metals from impurities</term>. This is because this "earth" is hot and dry, a symbol of fire, and therefore dries out the moisture of the matter. The rest is clear enough and has been sufficiently explained previously.

Take the very pure air, the colored fire, and the radiant water, and mix them. Our dung <note>original: "fumier." In alchemy, "dung" often refers to the base matter undergoing putrefaction, or sometimes to the gentle, moist heat of a manure pile used for digestion.</note> is quicksilver <term>quicksilver: (argent vif) the common name for mercury</term>, and it is so called because its natural moisture (by reason of its oiliness) is preserved for a long time from putrefaction by its own heat. Now, the Philosophers have attributed several names to the matter because of the various degrees of cooking; for when Mercury is cold and moist, it is called Soul; when the fire has consumed its moisture and this same Mercury is dry, it is called Spirit; and furthermore, when it is fixed by a greater decoction <term>decoction: the process of heating a substance in a liquid to extract its essence or change its state</term>, it is called Body. Thus, one and the same thing is called by three different names. From an old manuscript.

### Scholium.

Here is a Master who in appearance speaks in a manner unlike the others, though he does not; saying that the dissolution of bodies is twofold. We have already said that dissolution is the separation of the parts or of the virtue of bodies—as with a tree that one separates into bark, trunk, leaves, and other parts, and from these same parts one extracts water, oil, salt, and earth by the alembic <term>alembic: a distillation apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube</term> or by fire. The first dissolution necessary for this work is into mercury—that is to say, into blackness, or if one prefers, into liquid matter to which the sun <note>Gold</note> and the moon <note>Silver</note> are reduced by the amalgam of the first mercury. This is altogether nothing but a common confusion or mixture, through which one arrives at this second Mercury or first Saturn <note>In this context, Saturn refers to the "Lead of the Philosophers" or the black state of the matter, not common lead.</note> by the aid of a gentle fire; and this solution is only for particulars, name- <note>The text cuts off mid-word: "asça-" for *asçavoir* (namely).</note>

Our Author teaches us that what the Philosophers call *latten* <term>latten: original French *laton*; in alchemy, this refers to a base metal or an impure "blackened" alloy that must be purified until it shines like gold</term> is nothing common, nor a composite as many imagine. But just as red copper, when melted with calamine <note>a zinc-bearing mineral used in the historical production of brass</note> or calamite, loses its redness and becomes yellow, so too the latten of the Philosophers—which is *a body composed of the Sun <note>Gold</note> and Moon <note>Silver</note>*, and which he calls *copper with Mercury*—loses its luster and indeed its name. It is then neither gold nor silver, neither Sun nor Moon, but everything. For the first, namely the *latten*, is nothing other than the union of the two bodies; but the second, which is the *copper* <note>original: *l'airain*</note>, is the body ready to be dissolved. 

Let it not be thought a matter of doubt when he says "or," for it is as if he said: *latten* is what some have called by such a name, and not by another. But here is a question of little difficulty: namely, whether *sulfur* and *latten* are different things. To this one may answer that *latten* is the composition, and acts as the "ore" from which the sulfur emerges. Here, *sulfur* is taken not to mean the blackness <note>the *nigredo* or initial stage of decay</note>, but the whiteness or redness. Because this sulfur is still volatile <note>meaning it would evaporate or change if heat were applied</note>, one must join to it *the leaven*—that is to say, the Sun or the Moon—as will be seen hereafter in its proper place.

# CHAPTER I.

<meta>Catchword: [sc]iences; handwritten number 167 in margin; ink bleed from reverse page</meta>

### ->*TEXT*<-

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
Pay little heed to the words of modern or ancient Philosophers when they speak of this science, for the entirety of the art consists in the capacity of the intellect and in demonstrative experience. Because the Philosophers wished to hide the truths of the science, they have described all things by speaking in figures <note>original: "figures"; referring to metaphors, allegories, or symbolic diagrams</note>. Thomas to Brother Reynaud, Chapter 1. <note>This refers to a work traditionally attributed to Thomas Aquinas addressed to his companion, Reginald of Piperno.</note>

### ->*Scholia*<-

<margin>Note all of this carefully</margin>
This is yet another lesson for those who cling to the literal words and to the "bark" <note>the outer surface or superficial meaning of a text</note> without wishing to penetrate any deeper. It shows briefly that both the young and the old have set themselves to hiding this science. Though it is a natural science (as we have already stated), it must be carefully researched, pursued, and grasped by the spirit and by reason. It is reason that must judge, for example, whether a man can be begotten from the seed of a dog, or if a rabbit could grow from the germ of a mallow plant <note>a common flowering herb</note>, or if a volatile <term>volatile: a substance that easily evaporates or escapes when heated</term> thing can engender something manageable and fixed <term>fixed: a substance that remains stable and solid even when exposed to intense fire</term>. Reason must judge how a completely new thing can be made from another even newer thing, without the destruction of that first new thing, but rather its preservation. Indeed, it is necessary that the spirit be at play, and that reason—which is the mistress of all experiences—works just as powerfully.

<vocab>Philosophers, intellect, demonstrative experience, Thomas to Brother Reynaud, natural science, reason</vocab>

<summary>This page warns the reader against literal interpretations of alchemical texts, emphasizing that the "art" relies on intellectual reasoning and practical experience rather than the cryptic "figures" used by ancient philosophers. It argues that while alchemy is a natural science, it requires a sharp mind to distinguish between natural possibilities and absurdities.</summary>
<keywords>Thomas Aquinas, Brother Reginald, allegory, reason vs. experience, natural science, volatile and fixed, intellect, alchemical symbols</keywords>

*The primary matter of bodies is not **common mercury** <note>original: "mercure vulgaire"; the standard quicksilver available to merchants, which alchemists viewed as "dead" compared to their "living" Philosophic Mercury</note>, but it is an unctuous and moist vapor: for the **mineral stone** is made from the moist, and the metallic body from the unctuous; and it is necessary that the bodies be converted into such an unctuous vapor. This vapor is called the "stone," known through our books as the principle of the matter of our operation and **unctuous sulfur**, from which the **quintessence** <term>The "fifth essence" or purest spiritual core of a substance</term> is first extracted, and the mercury dyeing every body into **Sun** or **Moon** <note>Common alchemical code for Gold and Silver</note>, according to how it is prepared at the very end. The same [author], page 180.*

*Our stone is composed of body, spirit, and soul; for the imperfect body is called "body," the leaven is called "soul," and the water is called "spirit." The imperfect body is by its nature heavy, infirm, and dead; the water is a spirit that purges, refines, and whitens the body; the leaven is the soul which gives life to the imperfect body—a life it did not have before—and gives it a better form. The body is **Venus** <note>Symbolizing copper or the receptive, female principle in the chemical marriage</note> and female.*

The Philosophers have given several names to the stone, to the end that while it is manifest to the wise, the foolish do not know it; but however it may be named, it is always one, and of the same matter. The same [author], page 256.

->Scholium<-
<note>A scholium is a marginal note or explanatory commentary on a text.</note>

Our present Author tells us that even though several names are given to the matter, it is nonetheless not multiple, but unique and originating from one and the same thing; this is what the aforementioned sages have already noted. Now, if our matter did not come from another [source] that is pure and fixed, it could not be so itself: for one has never seen a bad tree produce good fruit, nor a fir tree produce oranges, nor a nettle a melon, since one cannot introduce into nature—that is to say, into a thing—anything that does not suit it; but since our matter emerges from another that is pure and fixed, the order of nature is that it should be so as well. It is true that the matters from which ours proceeds differ in species, such as the male and the female, but they agree in genus. Now, to show that the names do not make the thing different, he adds that *the juice of moonwort* <note>original: "suc de lunaire"; a plant (Botrychium lunaria) believed by alchemists to have lunar properties and used in "vegetable" alchemy</note>, *the water of life* <term>Eau de vie: literally "water of life"; here referring to a potent alchemical solvent or spirit rather than modern brandy</term>, *the quintessence of burning wine*, and *vegetable mercury* <note>The vital essence or "spirit" extracted from plant matter</note> are one and the same thing. **Magnesia** <note>In alchemy, "Magnesia" does not refer to the modern element magnesium, but to the "First Matter" or the crude, dark substance from which the Philosopher's Stone is extracted.</note> is the general matter containing the **four elements**; **mercury**, cooked in such a way that it has not lost its **fiery virtue**, is a perfect body without any exhalation <note>Meaning it has been stabilized so it no longer evaporates or "fumes" away when heated.</note>. It is a very clear thing that mercury will be perfected sooner by adding the **bodies** <note>Usually referring to the "perfect" metals, gold and silver.</note> to it than by remaining alone, which the Philosophers confirm, saying and calling the **Sun** <note>Gold</note> the brother of mercury and the **Moon** <note>Silver</note> its sister. And whoever joins me with my brother or my sister will nourish as many thousands of men for as long as he wishes, which he will achieve by making the male impregnate the female. *Book of the "The Lord be with you," p. 50.*

### Scholium.

If it is true (as indeed it is) that all the colors, and consequently the completion of our entire work, occur through a single process, why then are there so many vessels, so many furnaces, and so many various operations proposed by the charlatans? These men are totally ignorant of the intention and understanding of the wise <term>Philochymists</term> <note>From the Greek, meaning "lovers of chemistry/alchemy."</note>, who desire that from their composition there be produced a *black mud*, stinking, impalpable <note>Too fine to be felt as distinct particles.</note>, unctuous, and subtle. This mud, being washed with its own "water" (which it drinks and reduces, like itself, into an impalpable powder), turns white and then red; and having been whitened or reddened, it purifies the so-called "impure" metals. Now this mud, which is drawn from the two astralized and radiant bodies, is called *shadow* or *dryness* <note>original: "siccité"</note>, hidden within the bodies of the *Sun* <note>Symbolizing Gold.</note> and the *Moon* <note>Symbolizing Silver.</note> which have been made humid by the <term>amalgam</term> <note>A blend of metals, usually involving mercury.</note> to which the artist has reduced them. By this amalgam, the entire mass is rendered with a radiant whiteness and becomes as a single matter. This is the reason why he <note>Referring to Hermes, mentioned on the previous page.</note> does not say that one must draw the shadow from the "rays" [plural], but from "its ray" [singular]; showing that this *shadow* or *blackness* <note>The text ends mid-word with the catchword "noir-" (black-), indicating the continuation on the next page: "noirceur."</note> must come from the union of the two, and not from them separately.

### Scholium.

<margin>The reason for the names of things.</margin>
Everything that possesses a name has received it either from its Author, or from its place [of origin], or from its resemblance [to something else], or from its change, or from its specific property. This is the reason why so many different names have been given to this matter; the reasons for these I could provide easily enough, but such an explanation would be more subtle and laborious than useful to the seeker. When the seeker has finally found and come to enjoy his "beloved" <note>A common alchemical metaphor for the successful completion of the Great Work or the discovery of the Stone.</note>, he will clearly recognize the truth of how these names were assigned. ### Scholium <note>term: "Scholium"; a marginal note or explanatory commentary on a difficult text.</note>.

The beginning of the work is the assembly of our gold, silver & mercury, from which a blackness is produced, named the *raven's head* <note>original: "teste de corbeau"; also known as the *caput corvi*, this signifies the *Nigredo* or "blackening" stage, representing the death and putrefaction of the initial materials before they can be reborn.</note>. In this embrace, through a mutual love heated by a fire of friendship, this hidden blackness appears—but not in a crucible or by a melting fire, as the ignorant believe. Now, this entire compound or generating mass is not the *Corfusle* <note>term: "Corfusle"; as noted previously, this refers to the "all-in-one" composite matter of the Stone.</note>, but that which is engendered, or the blackness, is the beginning of the work. This blackness must be separated from the matter, as will be shown hereafter in its proper place. Once separated, it must be watered—which he calls *burning* in order to deceive the ignorant—*seven times* (a finite number used for an indefinite one) <note>In alchemy, "seven times" often implies "repeatedly" or "as many times as necessary" to achieve the desired perfection, rather than a literal count of seven.</note>. That is to say, as many times as will be necessary to bring it to whiteness. And then it will tint any body fit to receive its tincture; for to understand "any body" plainly, this general word would exclude nothing in the world, as will be shown in the chapter on projection <note>term: "Projection"; the final stage of the Great Work where the Philosopher's Stone is cast onto a base metal to transform it into gold or silver.</note>.

He adds that even though *rusting is a feigned name*, it is nevertheless true that this "rusting" is the second work or operation, namely the blackness. For the mixing or assembly is the first operation, and this rust or blackness is called the second because, after this composition, it appears over the entire compound. He says this is made from gold alone, in the same sense that one says a man makes a child without naming the woman. And this *rusting* (he says) was hidden within the sulphur, that is to say...

...and the final sprinkling <note>original: *irroration*; the alchemical process of moistening a dry substance with a liquid, often compared to dew falling on grass.</note>, it is the spirit of mercury alone. In the Ninth Exercise of the Tomb <note>Likely a reference to the 9th Dictum of the *Turba Philosophorum* (The Assembly of the Philosophers); "tombe" was occasionally used as a corruption of "turbe" in early French manuscripts.</note>.

By saying *the air must be cooked*, etc., he means that when the blackness is whitened—which he calls *air*—one must neither feed it further nor ferment it to lead it toward the red color, but merely continue the fire. Once this red color arrives—which he calls *sublimation* <note>In this context, sublimation refers to the "exaltation" or spiritualization of the matter as it reaches its highest state, rather than just the physical transition from solid to gas.</note>—it will be mixed with *its luminous body*. These two luminaries are called *leaven or fermentation*; and when the whole is completed, it is called *spirit*, because by its subtlety it penetrates the metals with which it is composed. From two things differing in nature—namely, a subtle one and a coarse one—an entirely different whole is created.

# CHAPTER I.
<meta>catchword: of the Scot.</meta>

<margin>
...division remains in you inseparably, namely through Wisdom. The same author, p. 312.

->Scholium.<-

This term **foliated earth** <note>original: *terre feuillee*; also known in Latin as *terra foliata*, it refers to the purified alchemical earth or the "salt" of the matter when it begins to crystallize into leaf-like flakes.</note> has caused great trouble for thousands of people. Some take it to mean bricks or tiles, others metals or ores, others the leaves and bark of trees; and without wishing to open their eyes, they throw themselves into inextricable confusion. 

Now, the Sages called the **small furnace** they used "foliated earth," because just as leaves protect fruit from external injury, so too is their matter preserved by and within it. Trevisan <note>Bernard of Trevisan (1406–1490), a famous Italian alchemist.</note> says in this regard that the fountain (which is the entirety of the matter within the matrass <note>A long-necked glass flask used for digestion and distillation.</note>) had been placed in a "hollow of oak," which is a wooden box. Another calls the matrass "foliated earth" for the same reason, and another calls mercury "foliated earth" because it envelops and covers all the metals from which the blackness <note>The *nigredo* or black stage, the initial phase of decomposition in the Great Work.</note> emerges. 

And others—indeed the majority—take the blackness floating atop the compound to be the "foliated earth," which, like a garment or mask, covers with its ugliness the most beautiful thing we need, which is the **white** or the **red** <note>The *albedo* (white) and *rubedo* (red) stages representing the purification and final perfection of the Philosopher's Stone.</note>. This is clearly indicated by this author. As for the saying that Adam brought it from Paradise, and that "man is its mine" <note>An alchemical aphorism suggesting that the raw materials for the Stone are found within the human being or are common to all.</note>, this was discussed in the previous scholium on the text of the Scot <note>Likely Michael Scot (c. 1175–1232), a scholar and translator whose name was often associated with medieval alchemical treatises.</note>.

<summary>This page explains the various metaphorical interpretations of the alchemical term "foliated earth," clarifying that it refers to the protective environment of the work or the initial "black" stage of the matter.</summary>

...pure substance and branches, those sensible things in others, and like unto them: Among these compounds, there are some which, it is believed, did not begin from a seed, but truly they grow and live secretly, multiply and are born. And what prevents them (namely the metals) from producing their like, from engendering, and from being able to convert [other substances] into themselves, is that their **vivifying spirit** is submerged and hindered by too much matter. This spirit is what Art <note>In this context, "Art" refers to Alchemy—the human skill used to perfect or accelerate natural processes.</note> can extract, it being certain that since every soul is incorporated, and that the whole world and its parts have bodies, there must be a middle spirit between these two things, which can be called neither soul nor body, but partakes of both; and it is this spirit that desires the multiplication of that in which it resides.

Now, gold among all metals is abundant in this spirit, which our Author names the ***incombustible grain, radical moisture, and seed***. This seed multiplies marvelously in the mine, and in each according to its property, sooner or later, Nature working there incessantly both by night and by day, which he calls here **Sun and Moon**. But if the learned Artist draws this **seed**—called by many **sulfur** <note>Alchemical sulfur represents the active, masculine, and combustible principle within a substance, not necessarily the chemical element sulfur.</note>—from it and joins it with its **glaire** <note>original: *glaire*; literally "egg white." In alchemy, this refers to the viscous, clear mercurial fluid that acts as the "womb" or medium for the sulfurous seed.</note>, he will have in a short time what nature cannot do alone in several hundred years; always remembering that this work is natural, and therefore one must proceed gently, for nature abhors violence.

<note>This passage argues that metals are not "dead" matter but possess a hidden life force or "seed" that allows them to grow in the earth. The alchemist's role is to remove the "excess matter" that stifles this growth, allowing the metal to reproduce or "multiply" rapidly in the laboratory.</note>

Many have been extremely troubled to find out what this <term>Elixir</term> <note>Elixir: from the Arabic "al-iksir," referring to a medicinal or transformative substance capable of changing base metals into gold or healing the human body.</note> is. ### Notice from the Scholiast <note>A scholiast is a scholar who writes explanatory notes or commentaries on a text.</note>.

I did not wish to dwell on giving a clearer understanding of any of the passages cited in this second chapter, since we are about to enter another, in which we will clarify many things; it is enough to have shown that the *Philosophers* <note>The ancient masters of alchemy.</note> never intended that there were different ways to reach the desired goal. ->HARM. CHYM. CH. II.<-

...and that no one can go to the Father except through him: <note>Referring to the previous page's quote of John 14:6: "No man cometh unto the Father, but by me." The author uses this to argue that just as there is only one way to salvation, there is only one way to the Great Work.</note> one might object to me that Mirandulanus <note>Giovanni Francesco Pico della Mirandola (1469–1533), an Italian philosopher and author of *De Auro* (On Gold), a famous Renaissance text on alchemy.</note> writes that he saw a man who had more than twenty ways of making gold. I reply that this conclusion is foolish, for the one of whom he speaks could mix his powder or "little stone" <note>The Philosopher's Stone.</note> with alum, sulfur, wax, tallow, soap, and other such materials, which vanished into mixed smoke when thrown upon the metals—whether already melted or about to be melted—and only the **staining** and **fixed Medicine** <note>The "Tincture." Alchemists believed the Stone acted as a "Medicine" that cured "sick" (base) metals by staining them with the color and permanence of gold.</note> remained with these metals, which it colored and fixed. But if Mirandulanus had said he had seen an infinity of entirely different materials from which, or by which, the metals were transmuted, that would be another matter; but he does not say so. And even if it were so, his authority would have no force against so many weighty Authors. Let us then cut it short and say with the *Philosophers* <note>The traditional masters of the alchemical art.</note> that there is **only one path, one matter, one vessel, and one fire**; and all those who seek more, or seek others, are deluding themselves and deceiving those who believe them. Like the blind, both the leader and the led will fall into the pit <note>original: "precipice"</note> of regret, and perhaps of shame. As for us, we shall be content to follow and show the desired path, which will reveal to us the necessary materials.

If all things are made of the matter to which they are reduced, there is no difficulty in accepting that metals are made of mercury. This is the reason why **Thomas** <note>Likely referring to Pseudo-Thomas Aquinas, the name under which several influential alchemical treatises were written in the Middle Ages.</note> along with the other **Philosophers** <note>In this context, "Philosophers" refers specifically to alchemists, the "Philosophers of Fire."</note> tells us that mercury alone completes our work; this is to exclude any other matter that is corrosive or destructive to metals. Mercury, therefore, truly dissolves the **Sun** <note>Alchemical term for Gold.</note> and the **Moon** <note>Alchemical term for Silver.</note>. I say "dissolves," which is to say it draws or pulls out from their bodies, by means of the **Artist's** <note>The practitioner or alchemist performing the work.</note> help, a matter which is neither Sun nor Moon, and can never be so.

Just as from the male and the female comes a matter or sperm which is neither male nor female, and can never be that specific man or woman from whom the matter issued—but rather something resembling one or the other—likewise, that which comes out of this Sun and Moon by means of mercury, aided by a suitable heat, will never be and cannot be (whatever artifice one applies to it) Sun and Moon. This happens without any loss to the quality of the Sun; the Sun and Moon find themselves diminished only by the weight of that extracted matter. 

Let those, therefore, who wish to practice this admirable work learn that our **dissolution** is not the kind understood by those who merely compile recipes. Let them also learn to understand our words and terms, without which they will never be able to properly understand the intention of the Philosophers who have written expressly regarding this science. Now, says our Author, the gold and silver—which are called "domestics," the brother and sister of the said mercury—must be dissolved, that is to say re-

### Scholium. <note>original: "Scholie." A scholium is an explanatory note or commentary intended to clarify a specific point in a text.</note>

Each thing begets its like; for if one extracts mercury from lead, that which is produced will result in lead. This extraction, therefore, will not be what we seek, nor is it the "egg" understood here, which is composed of good materials—namely, of purified and healthy gold and silver covered with crude mercury <note>Crude mercury refers to "virgin" mercury found naturally in its liquid state, rather than mercury chemically "revived" from ore by man.</note>—specifically that which comes directly from the mine, but very clean, which will serve as the skin [of the egg]. The whole is placed in a glass vessel, which will be the hard shell, beneath which one shall place a proper fire. 

O seekers and lovers of truth, I conjure you by the truth that I adore: flee and banish far from you all these extractors of mercury from lead. For although the Philosophers <note>In this context, "the Philosophers" refers to the established authorities of the alchemical tradition, such as Hermes Trismegistus or Geber.</note> say that one must extract mercury from Saturn <note>Saturn is the traditional alchemical name and symbol for the metal lead.</note>—which many call lead—I assure you, upon the oath I have sworn to truth itself, that it must not be understood as common lead, but as the "Lead of the Philosophers." Those who do not believe me will be deceived; and <margin>*Reasons for the scholium.*</margin> I protest that nothing makes me bring these writings to light but the charity and compassion I have upon seeing so many good people deceived by these rascally vagabonds. These men promise those who listen to them mountains of gold, and yet they have not the means to sustain or clothe themselves, which is easy to see by their actions.

### Scholium.

Each generates its own kind; so that if one extracts mercury from lead, this offspring will produce lead. Therefore, this extraction is not what we seek, nor is the "egg" understood here in that way. This egg is composed of good materials—namely, of purified and very healthy gold and silver, covered with raw mercury <note>In alchemy, the "egg" refers to the sealed glass vessel and its contents, symbolizing the gestation of the Philosopher's Stone.</note> that comes directly from the mine, yet is very clean, which will serve as the skin. For although the Philosophers say that one must draw mercury from Saturn <note>original: "Saturne." In alchemical symbolism, Saturn represents the metal lead.</note>, which many call lead, I assure you—by the oath I have sworn to truth itself—that this must not be understood as common lead <note>The author is distinguishing between "vulgar" lead (the physical metal) and "philosophical" lead (a specific state of matter or a different substance altogether).</note>, but as the lead of the Philosophers. Whoever does not believe me will be deceived. ### Scholium.

Though Alanus speaks of "transparent water," one must not, however, imagine a water through which one can see <note>The author is warning the reader not to expect a literal liquid like tap water.</note>, for this goes against the opinion of all the Philosophers, who desire only materials that symbolize <note>To "symbolize" here means to have a shared natural affinity or a "sympathy" of substance.</note> together; for what proportion would there be between wetting water <note>Common water that wets the hands.</note> and gold and silver? Moreover, no wetting water can dissolve gold and silver, seeing as the <term>philosophical dissolution <note>A process where a metal is reduced to its primary, liquid-like state without losing its "soul" or essential nature, unlike chemical dissolution in acids.</note></term> consists in reducing them to their principle, which is volatile, without them ever being able to be what they had been before, as we have stated previously. He therefore understands by this word "transparent"—meaning clear and shining—<term>common mercury <note>Quicksilver.</note></term> that has been very well purified, into which he intends for the gold and silver to be placed. I am not ignorant of the power of strong water— <note>original: "l’eau for-", completed by the catchword "te" as "eau forte," or nitric acid.</note>

->Scholium.<-

Our author begins with the response that one is accustomed to making to a question such as this: "What do you wish to have in your garden?" Answer: "Cabbages, lettuce, and the like." Question: "And why then do you not take the seed of cabbages and lettuce?" Now, it is the case that the seed only proceeds from its plant, therefore it must be drawn from it. Likewise, he who wants to have gold, silver, iron, copper, brass, or lead, must draw from them their seed, which is commonly called <term>mercury</term> <note>In alchemical theory, Mercury is the "feminine" principle of fluidity and transformation, not merely the common liquid metal.</note> or <term>sulfur</term> <note>Sulfur represents the "masculine" principle of combustion, structure, and color.</note> by similarity of property. <header>CHAPTER III.</header>

...metempsychosis <note>original: *teplychose* (likely a corruption of *metempsychose*); the Pythagorean doctrine of the transmigration of souls from one body to another.</note> of Pythagoras, who held that a soul, upon leaving the body in which it lived, should enter the first empty body it encountered. Our author adds that this happens by means of its spirit—otherwise nothing is accomplished—and yet, in all of this, there is only **form** and **matter**, **brother** and **sister**, **agent** and **patient**, which the ancient Philosophers have named the **composition**. This composition contains **dryness** in the third degree, **humidity** in the second, **coldness** in the first, and a **slackened heat** <note>original: *chaleur remise*; a gentle or moderated heat, rather than an intense, direct flame.</note>. For if this heat were at the beginning of the fourth degree, it would follow that it would burn everything, and we would have no need for external fire. But insofar as this heat is a slave, it must be set at liberty; he who does not understand this should study. Regardless, having disengaged this slow and slackened heat, we render it supreme; but dryness follows it, and these two, once united, bend the rebel <note>Likely referring to the volatile or "moist" element that resists stabilization.</note> to their will and put the prisoner to death. Consequently, the **crown** remains without controversy for this first slave <note>The "slave" (internal heat) becomes the "king" or "crowned" principle after being liberated and refined.</note>. 

But if one sets the heat one degree lower, dryness at the second degree, humidity at the first, and a slackened coldness, it will come to give us contentment. However, it will provide much more if the cold takes the upper hand of the two lower points, and humidity the two highest, with heat at the third degree, dryness at the second, and humidity at the first of the two points; this will be the **completed work**. But this shall be made clear when we speak of numbers and figures.

The **mercury** in which **gold** and **silver** have been dissolved is considered by some to be the **double mercury** of which **Trevisan** <note>Bernard of Trevisan (1406–1490) was a legendary Italian alchemist whose writings emphasized the use of mercury and gold.</note> speaks in his *Epistle to **Thomas of Bologna*** <note>Thomas of Bologna was the physician to King Charles V of France and a fellow alchemist.</note>. Thus, from the two, a certain third thing is made, which is neither one nor the other, but something else entirely, holding the nature of both.

Now experience, which is the teacher of everyone, shows (as has already been said) that everything under the concavity of the heavens is **combustible** and **volatile**, with only **gold** and **silver** excepted. The matter of the <term>Philosophers</term> <note>A term for alchemists, the "Philosophers of Nature."</note> is water, and this refers to the water of these three [components], and one needs neither more nor less. The **Sun** is the male, the **Moon** the female, and **mercury** the seed. But for the end that generation and conception may take place, the male must join the female, and besides this the seed is required; therefore, before <term>fermentation</term> <note>The stage where the "leaven" of gold or silver is added to the base matter to direct its transformation.</note>, the conception and impregnation must be performed. When the matter multiplies, it is said that the child grows in the mother’s womb; when it ferments, the soul is infused into the body, and the **Crowned King** grows. Dissolve the bodies and imbibe the spirit. One speaks of "bodies" in the plural because at least two are needed, and "spirit" in the singular because one suffices; and there is no seed without the matter of a body other than mercury. When one says "imbibe the spirit," this refers to the operation which fixes the mercury and multiplies the stone; to multiply is the same as to say to reiterate. The same [author], p. 204.

He will learn that fire is hot essentially and dry accidentally; air is moist essentially and hot by accident; water is moist essentially and cold by accident; and earth is dry essentially, but cold accidentally. <note>In Aristotelian physics, "essential" qualities are the primary nature of an element, while "accidental" qualities are secondary traits that allow elements to transform into one another.</note> Let no one therefore believe that this art belongs to just anyone, but rather to a person consumed by study, whose spirit does not turn with every wind, but who, having laid a good foundation, builds upon it and tests all the spirits who come to whisper in his ear, promising mountains of gold while wandering as naked wretches, hungry and poor, from place to place. <note>original: "chauds nuds." *Gold alone is the <term>leaven<gloss>original: "levain"; in alchemy, a substance added to a base "dough" to catalyze its transformation, much like yeast in bread-making.</gloss></term> of the red elixir, and silver [the leaven] of the white [elixir], and to these two alone nature has distributed its rays of splendor, by which the other metals may be illustrated with the beauty of gold and silver. All the other metals must be taken as the dough or the matter of the <term>stone<gloss>The Philosopher's Stone, the legendary goal of alchemy said to transform base metals into noble ones.</gloss></term>, and can never be taken for the form or the leaven, unless they are first ennobled to such a degree and for so long that the production of gold and silver is the goal of Chemistry; for if the production of iron were the end proposed in Chemistry, then the form or the leaven would be iron; now just as gold is the leaven of gold, and silver [is the leaven] of silver, so iron would be the leaven of iron, tin of tin, copper of copper, and lead of lead; for every agent acts according to its form. The same [author], page 296.*

All the *Philosophers* <note>In alchemical texts, "Philosophers" refers to the practitioners of the "Hermetic Philosophy," or alchemy.</note> assert that the <term>elixir<gloss>A preparation capable of changing base metals into gold or silver, also called the "Stone."</gloss></term> has three parts: namely, the soul, the body, and the spirit. This spirit is nothing other than that liquor which subtilizes and renders the form and the matter of the stone into a spiritual nature; this spirit is sometimes called by the *Philosophers* "heaven," "dissolving mercury," <term>menstruum<gloss>A solvent, particularly one that can dissolve gold or other metals.</gloss></term>, <term>azoth<gloss>A term for the essential agent of transformation, often identified with mercury.</gloss></term>, <term>quintessence<gloss>The "fifth essence" or purest part of a substance.</gloss></term>, and an infinity of other names. ### CHAPTER III.

...to render a <term>leper<gloss>In alchemical literature, a "leper" refers to an impure or "sick" base metal, such as lead or copper, which must be "healed" into the "healthy" perfection of gold.</gloss></term> strong; take then the gold and silver, and render them **Sun** and **Moon**, that is to say, very pure and very radiant. Such are named **sulfur** and **arsenic**; join them by the aid of **mercury**, and do not believe you can do it easily or promptly, but rather with some difficulty and length of time. For this joining is not a simple mixing, but a <term>physical union<gloss>The author uses "mixtion physique" to distinguish a deep chemical bonding from a mere mechanical mixture of ingredients.</gloss></term> to which separation never occurs, inasmuch as from heterogeneous things they are made homogeneous.

And then the **eyes**—that is to say, that which demonstrates the interior to us (for the eyes are the windows of the soul)—are **black**. This blackness having passed, the **feet**—that is to say, the second degree through which perfection passes—are **white**. This is the **whiteness**, which, continued in its proper heat, is converted into **redness**, which is the supreme state of all, just as the head is the highest part of the animal.

And then one has taken as the principle of the work—and without which nothing will advance—not the luminaires of the world <note>The "luminaires" are the actual Sun and Moon in the sky; the author warns that the alchemist needs the terrestrial "seeds" of these metals, not celestial light.</note>, but that which is homogeneous within them, that is to say, their **seed**. For whatever the artist may do, he cannot join the **Sun** with the **Moon** except through their seeds; once these are joined, man can never discern nor separate one seed from the other.

This union of seeds is therefore the true dissolution, the seed, and the true marriage. In the treatment of this marriage, and during their loves, the fiancé is totally transformed into the character of his fiancée; that is to say, the **gold** becomes white, wearing the livery of **Beya** <note>original: "liurees de Beya". A livery is a uniform worn by a servant; here it means the gold takes on the white color of the lunar principle.</note>. But after this union, Beya returns the favor to her **Gabriel**, transforming herself in all things into him.

### CHAPTER III.

->Scholium.<-
<note>A scholium is a marginal note or explanatory commentary on a text.</note>

The Philosophers say that mercury is made of an earthy matter, but more <term>subtle<gloss>In alchemy, "subtle" refers to matter that has been refined, purified, or rendered into a more gaseous or spiritual state.</gloss></term> than ash or lime, and of a moisture thinner than water, which Aristotle says is an aqueous and earthy vapor; they say that these two matters are so subtilized and exactly mixed that the smallest part of one enters into the smallest part of the other, and thus from the two, one is made. This opinion is held by Democritus, Gilgil, <note>Possibly a reference to Al-Jildaki or another medieval alchemical authority often cited alongside Greek philosophers.</note> and Plato. The elixir must resemble this <term>quicksilver<gloss>From the French "argent vif" (living silver). It refers here not to common mercury, but to the philosophical principle of fluidity and transformation.</gloss></term>, for to compose the elixir, one takes a fixed substance and a volatile one, and must so subtilize and mix these two substances that they become only one, which shall be named *quicksilver, or the perfect secret*—that is to say, the stone or matter of the Philosophers. This is the final effect of the fire, namely to make this matter red, into which the mercury—added to this <term>homogeneity<gloss>A state where different substances are perfectly blended into a single, uniform nature.</gloss></term> (which is the hidden body)—is reduced. This perfected matter is called the *mercury that must be drawn from the quicksilver of the bodies*, that is to say, from gold and silver, by the order already marked, and which will be marked again in the chapter on Operations.

### CHAPTER III.

->Scholia<-

<margin>fol: Florentius</margin> The Sage tells us that one must answer nothing to the fool, so that one is not esteemed [to be like him], as the same [author] tells us; <note>This is a reference to the biblical proverb (Proverbs 26:4): "Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest thou also be like unto him."</note> for the greater part of seekers, having placed an opinion—whatever it may be—in their brains, attach themselves to it so firmly that they believe no one else has the true knowledge of the stone but themselves, and nothing can divert them but the end, which they find to be entirely contrary to their goal. They will never have anything (says our author) if they do not join the <term>Sun<gloss>Representing gold, or the fixed, masculine principle.</gloss></term> and the <term>Moon<gloss>Representing silver, or the volatile, feminine principle.</gloss></term> to make one body of them by means of the water, which is <term>mercury<gloss>The fluid metal used as a universal solvent and mediating spirit in alchemical operations.</gloss></term>, which by its force (which he calls spirit) unites the white and red earth (which is gold and silver) with itself. Now, in this composition, a <term>blackness<gloss>The *nigredo* stage, often described as the "crow's head," signifying the death and putrefaction of the materials before their rebirth.</gloss></term> occurs, which some believe to be a filthiness proceeding either from the mercury or from the bodies plunged therein; and consequently, they remove it by blowing, washing, and re-washing; but the more they wash the entire mass, the more the whole becomes blackened, so that the total is reduced to loss, and thus they find themselves deceived. Let this blackness be guided by the mercury, and then let it be nourished by its earth; and by these three (which he calls juices), nature and the artist shall engender, nourish, and complete the <term>elixir<gloss>The final transformative substance of the Great Work.</gloss></term>.

->*Scholium.*<- <note>A scholium is an explanatory note or commentary on a text.</note>

The <term>Chemical Philosophers<gloss>The term used for alchemists who studied the transformation of matter.</gloss></term> call "fixed" any metal that resists all trials by fire, such as the <term>ash-test<gloss>A method of refining gold or silver using a bed of ashes.</gloss></term> or <term>cupel<gloss>A shallow, porous bowl used in assaying to separate precious metals from lead and other impurities.</gloss></term>, or the <term>royal cement<gloss>A dry refining process used to purify gold by heating it with salts and acids.</gloss></term> usually composed of rubified vitriol <note>Iron sulfate heated until it turns red.</note>, burnt verdigris, <term>sal ammoniac<gloss>Ammonium chloride, a salt used as a flux in metalworking.</gloss></term>, brick, and emery. Some compose it differently using the "royal water of departure" or <term>aqua fortis<gloss>Literally "strong water," referring to nitric acid.</gloss></term> made from two pounds of Roman vitriol, one pound of saltpeter, and one pound of alum, each prepared accordingly. This acid turns the <term>Moon<gloss>The alchemical name for silver.</gloss></term> into water <note>meaning it dissolves the silver into a liquid solution</note> but not gold; however, if one adds sal ammoniac to this aqua fortis, it is then called <term>aqua regia<gloss>Latin for "royal water," a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids.</gloss></term>, and it turns gold into water. From these two bodies resolved into water, an admirable secret is drawn—sought and sought again, yet little known. It is a key without which few people enter into this satisfaction; for although this key opens [the door], it does not enter the house itself. Among all the metals, only gold maintains itself there, for silver withstands only the cupel, while the others are consumed by it. Many <note>original: "se rompent la teste" — literally "break their heads," meaning to struggle or exhaust oneself with a difficult problem.</note> trouble themselves trying to "fix" silver because they find it written in books, but it is in vain; for the silver of which the authors write is the "white matter" that the Philosophers call <term>fixed silver</term>. One must take common silver, very well purified, which is not fixed; added to fixed gold, these make a matter between the two, not being at the beginning so...

...will be the eagle <gloss>the eagle</gloss> <note>In alchemy, the "eagle" often symbolizes the volatile spirit or the process of sublimation.</note>, and this slowness will unite and homogenize the two substances that are seemingly contrary, namely this black sulfur and the **celestial mercury** <term>celestial mercury<gloss>A purified, subtle form of mercury believed to contain the "spirit of the world."</gloss></term>; the blackness being a hot and dry powder, and the mercury being cold and moist. But someone might say that this blackness comes from the filth and excrement of the impure materials of the compound; to which we respond that the **Sun** <note>Gold.</note>, the **Moon** <note>Silver.</note>, and **mercury** have been rendered such as we call "astralized" <note>Elevated to a higher, more potent "celestial" state through chemical refinement.</note> by an exact depuration <note>The process of purging impurities.</note>. Since that is the case, this blackness does not proceed from their filth, as none has remained in them; furthermore, if it were filth and excrement, it would be consumed by the fire and would not mix exactly with its milk <note>The "Virgin’s Milk," a common alchemical term for a white mercurial solvent or the dissolving liquid of the work.</note>, nor would it be nourished or increase therein. For dregs and filth do not receive nourishment; yet this black matter does receive it. Therefore, it is not an excrement, unless one understands it in the same way that Physicians say human seed is, which they define as being the "excrement of the final concoction" <note>In the medical tradition of Galen and Aristotle, "concoction" refers to the body "cooking" nutrients; reproductive fluid was thought to be the final, most refined surplus (or "excrement") of the blood-purification process.</note>. <margin>Alanus</margin>
**H**e who knows not how to draw the soul of the **Sun** and of the **Moon** <note>Sun and Moon: Traditional alchemical symbols for Gold and Silver.</note>, and to restore that same soul to the body by **projection** <term>projection<gloss>The final stage of the Great Work, where the Alchemical Stone is cast upon base metals to transform them into gold or silver.</gloss></term>, let him know that he is heavily mistaken. The extraction of the soul by the spirit of mercury is not performed all at once, but in several stages—that is to say, at various times, days, hours, and moments—until one has a sufficient amount of it. The soul is not drawn from the bodies all at once, but through many [iterations]; nor does the vessel containing the dissolution (that is, the vessel in which the body dissolves) allow the matter to dissolve there all at once. Rather, it happens from one day to the next, little by little, and once again, little by little, following the regimen of the worker and of nature. Do not think, therefore, that the solution of the body occurs in a single instance, but little by little through the passage of time, and according to what the Philosophers have said and what their writings testify. Do not believe that the **tincture** <term>tincture<gloss>The spiritual essence or "color" of the metal that carries its transformative power.</gloss></term> is drawn in a single instance, but rather diligently, little by little, and again little by little; that is to say, a blackness [from] day... <note>original: "noirceur". The text ends mid-sentence; the catchword "par" (by) indicates the next page likely continues "day by day".</note>

### Scholium <note>original: *Scholie*. An explanatory commentary or note on a text.</note>

Many who are ignorant of our composition are also ignorant of our dissolution, and consequently ignore the extraction of the dissolved matter, called the **Soul** <note>In alchemy, the "Soul" refers to the volatile essence or the "tincture" that gives metal its properties.</note>, which is this **blackness** <note>The "blackness" or *nigredo* is the first major stage of the Great Work, representing putrefaction and the breakdown of matter.</note> of which we have already spoken, and which can be collected every eight days, more or less, according to the diligence and skill of the artist. Now, because at least one ounce of it is needed, and because it will take a long time to produce if one takes too little matter, it would be wise to take a significant quantity—such as four ounces of each of the two bodies, which will make eight ounces, and thirty-two ounces of **marine water** or **mercury** <note>original: *eau marine ou mercure*. This refers to the "mercurial solvent" used to break down the metals.</note>. These forty ounces can provide the desired ounce in about three months, or one hundred days. Once this is extracted, the mercury will be found at its original weight—provided care was taken that none of it was lost—and the two bodies will be diminished only by the amount that the extracted blackness weighs. These bodies will remain as good and beautiful as they were before they were mixed, and Goldsmiths and **Refiners** <note>original: *Rafineurs*. Professionals skilled in purifying precious metals.</note> know how to separate them from one another, which they do by means of **aqua fortis** <term>aqua fortis<gloss>Literally "strong water"; nitric acid, used to dissolve silver and separate it from gold.</gloss></term>. O curious seeker! Man and woman, after having surrendered and mixed their seed and cast it into the **matrix** <term>matrix<gloss>The womb; in alchemy, this refers to the sealed vessel or the philosophical environment where generation occurs.</gloss></term>, are not themselves diminished afterward. Have you not yet learned in our books that this practice is very similar to generation?

<summary>This page provides a practical "scholium" or commentary on the extraction of the metallic "soul" (the blackness), detailing the specific weights of mercury and metal bodies required and the time needed for the process. It uses the analogy of human reproduction to explain how the "seeds" of metals can produce a new substance without the original bodies being permanently destroyed.</summary>

O seekers, to make a man, you do not take the earth from which God formed man; rather, you take the seed which proceeds from the man, without the man himself being destroyed. To achieve this, the reading of good authors, subtle meditation, and patience in labor are necessary.

Take the calx <term>chaux</term> <note>A powder or "ash" produced by heating a metal to a high temperature (calcination).</note>, or the prepared and washed earth of each "imperfect body" <note>In alchemy, "imperfect bodies" refers to base metals like lead, tin, iron, or copper, as opposed to the "perfect" metals, gold and silver.</note>, and place in it some similarly purified mercury, until it floats above the powder by two or three fingers’ breadth in a long vessel having a narrow neck. This oil must be separated and set aside. Then, repeat the process as described above until all the oil is drawn out and nothing more is seen to rise. At that point, separate your mercury from the calx and place it upon the same quantity of purified calx from whatever metal you please. Proceed as before, continuing the slow fire until you have extracted all the vivifying moisture <term>humeur viuifiant</term> from it. You may repeat this operation as often as you wish—that is to say, until you have gathered the entire quantity of oil that you desire—adding new mercury if the amount you initially used has diminished. Finally, place all this collected oil into a cucurbit <term>cucurbite</term> <note>The lower part of a distilling apparatus, shaped like a gourd.</note>, and for every one part of oil, add six parts of the mercury that you used to extract the oil.

### CHAPTER IV.

Because goldsmiths working in jewelry say that they cannot work in gold at twenty-two carats without applying a remedy or alloy <term>alliage</term>, or in fine gold at a quarter of a remedy, they only work at twenty, and most often at nineteen carats; so that in twenty-four marks <term>marcs</term> <note>A traditional unit of weight for gold and silver, approximately 245 grams.</note>, they add five marks of either silver or copper. This is how the gold they put to work is not pure, and for an excuse they say it is impossible for refiners <term>affineurs</term> to refine gold to the twenty-fourth carat without there being some small amount of other metal added, nor silver to the 12th degree without there being some alloy. And even that the prescribed refinement according to the ordinance <term>ordonnance</term> <note>The official royal decree governing the standards for precious metals.</note> is only at twenty-three carats and 3 "carats of carats" <note>Subdivisions used for extreme precision in measuring fineness.</note>, on an 8th of remedy <term>remede</term> <note>The "remedy" was a legal allowance for a slight deviation in the weight or purity of coins and jewelry.</note>, and silver at eleven deniers <term>deniers</term> <note>A system of measuring silver purity where 12 deniers is absolute purity.</note> two grains and three carats, such as it is in Spanish reals <note>Spanish silver coins, known for their high quality and used as a standard of purity.</note>, or else eleven deniers eighteen grains, as it is at the Paris hallmark <term>poinçõ de Paris</term>. It is no wonder then that such gold and silver are called "imperfect," "impure," and "not ours" <note>In alchemy, "not ours" refers to common commercial metals that have not yet been "philosophically" prepared for the Great Work.</note>; but after having been well purified, they are called calcined <term>calcinez</term>. This is because this depuration of gold is done by parting water <term>eau du despart</term> <note>Nitric acid, which "parts" or separates silver and base metals from gold by dissolving them.</note>, which gnaws and reduces to water for a time everything that is not gold, or by antimony <term>antimoine</term> which consumes every metal other than gold; and silver is purified by the cupel <term>couppelle</term> <note>A shallow, porous vessel used in cupellation to separate precious metals from base metals through high heat.</note>. It is in this way that one must understand "lime" <term>chaux</term> <note>Commonly called 'calx'; the powdery, purified state of a metal after it has been refined or oxidized.</note>, without imagining an infinity of other useless operations described and invented by many, either through ignorance or to deceive the ignorant and the overly presumptuous. # CHEMICAL HARMONY

### Scholium.

Arnaldus <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note> has hidden the method for the dissolution of bodies, which this Author declares to us: namely, that it is by means of mercury, and that this mercury (specifically the "mercury of the Philosophers") is drawn from the bodies themselves. It is black in color, or a spirit—this very blackness is drawn out by the "crude spirit." This process takes place inside the "mine," which is to say, within a vessel that is very well-sealed and heated by a small fire.

This will be achieved when you have drawn part of his nature and part of the nature of his wife. Once that is done, kill them; and being dead, they shall rise again in a new resurrection, so that afterward they shall be immortal. *The Ladder of the Philosophers, p. 100.*

### CHAPTER IV.

...what is first in composition is last in resolution <note>A fundamental alchemical and Aristotelian principle: the process of breaking a substance down into its primary components (resolution) is the exact reverse of the process used to build it up (composition).</note>, and that the matter which is the most dense endures the greatest force, and resists its active and dissolving agent much more, and that every agent acts according to the strength of the resistant matter against which it must prevail. But if the Reader has no understanding of the writings of the Philosophers, let him know that he cannot work well, because he has not yet entered into the knowledge of their matter; and whoever rejects the reading of good books and takes another path—amusing themselves by listening to wanderers and charlatans, and by trying out various recipes—let him know that he is gravely mistaken.

<margin>Reading is necessary.</margin>
Therefore, let him read (even if some friend teaches him faithfully) the good authors; but let him know that a single book does not teach everything necessary in this science, but rather one book interprets or clarifies what is hidden and obscure in another. As proof of this, Raymond <note>Raymond Lully (c. 1232–1315), a Majorcan philosopher and logician to whom many alchemical works were later attributed.</note>, Bacon <note>Roger Bacon (c. 1214–1292), an English friar and philosopher known for his emphasis on empiricism.</note>, Albert <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and bishop who wrote extensively on the natural sciences.</note>, and Anaxagoras <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher who argued that all things were composed of infinitely small fragments; he was often cited by alchemists regarding the "seeds" of matter.</note> have taught weight and proportion, though still obscurely: Bacon in his *Epistles*, Raymond a little more clearly in his *General Art*. Many people think they have a very good understanding of these after reading them only once, in which they are mistaken; they do not know what they are doing at the beginning, and will not know what will happen at the end. They will find this end to be contrary to the work of God, by whose word alone (let it be made <note>original: "soit faict," the French translation of the Latin *fiat* from Genesis.</note>) and from no prior matter this entire universe was made; but the opposite happens to these surly men...

### CHAPTER IV.

...[re]ceive <note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing from the previous page's discussion of absorption.</note> a great quantity of food <note>original: *viande*; in this period, the term often referred to food in general, not just meat.</note> and drink, I eat and drink my fill of it, and the rest will be superfluous to me; the chyle <term>chile</term> <note>A milky fluid produced in the stomach during digestion.</note> which is formed in the ventricle or stomach, being agreeable to it, nourishes it; what remains as superfluity is sent to the intestines, so that what was superfluous to the stomach serves as food and nourishment to the liver.
