*The Assembly* <note>original: "Tourbe"; refers to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, written as a transcript of a debate among ancient philosophers.</note></margin>
If you do not break, rupture, soak, and diligently govern the body until you are able to extract its fat <note>In alchemy, "fat" or "oil" refers to the flammable, soulful essence or the "sulfur" hidden within the dry metal.</note>, and make of it a subtle and intangible spirit, you labor in vain. For this reason, the sages have said: if you do not make the bodies into non-bodies, and the spiritual things corporeal, you have not yet found the beginning of this work. Now, bodies are made into spirits when the <term>Ethel</term> <note>original: "Etelie"; a technical term used in the *Turba* to refer to the primary substance or the "spirit" of the matter, often associated with the black stage of the work.</note> is ground until it is turned into powder. This powder is not produced without strong grinding and continuous <term>decoction</term> <note>The process of heating a substance in a liquid to extract its essence; essentially a long, slow boiling.</note>, and it is accomplished with fire—not with the hands—through soaking, <term>putrefaction</term> <note>The stage where the matter "dies" and decays, turning black before it can be reborn in a purified state.</note>, and the Ethel. When the sages said, speaking of this art, that the "nature" <note>The starting material or "prime matter" of the work.</note> is vile and of little price, they caused the common people to go astray. The Philosophers have also said that the moist spirit is black but contains no filth; and just as humidity and dryness are found within man, so in our work there is nothing but vapor and water. *The Assembly*, dictum 37.

The Philosophers have said: know that if you do not reduce everything to powder, you have not yet ground it enough; cook, therefore, until everything is ground and made into powder. The same source, dictum 38.

The heavy, dross-like material or "dead earth" that remains after the spirit is extracted.</note> prevents the <term>multiplication</term> <note>The process of increasing the power and quantity of the finished Philosopher's Stone.</note> in quality, it must be removed. 

And thus one sees in how many ways the Authors understand this <term>superfluous</term> <note>original: "superflu." The "extra" or external matter that must be purged to reach the pure essence.</note> substance; all of these interpretations are true for those who understand them. However, all these interpretations cannot be grasped by a weak mind that is neither practical nor versed in the terms of this <term>science</term> <note>The "Sacred Science" of Alchemy.</note>. We are going to see a very great number of these terms, the majority of which are intended to sharpen the most subtle minds and to deceive the most overconfident.

<margin>the same [author] p. 103.</margin>
The way of acting, digesting, and informing <note>informing: in a philosophical sense, to give form or character to matter</note> belonging to art is different from that of nature, as are the organ—or the place—and the time; even so, they agree upon the same final goal. *The same author, p. 103.*

When the matter rises by means of the wind, that is to say by smoke <note>original: "la fumée"; likely referring to vapors or fumes within the alchemical vessel</note>, the Philosophers <note>Philosophers: a common term for alchemists or natural scientists of the era</note> have said that this is sublimation. And when the matter has been returned to the bottom of the vessel and converted into water, they have called it solution or distillation. When the earth has been thickened, they have called it corruption <note>corruption: here referring to the breakdown of a substance's previous form, a necessary stage before purification</note>. When the matter has begun to change its black color, they said that it was ablution <note>ablution: a washing or purification process</note>. The magistery <note>magistery: the mastery of the art, or the finished medicinal/alchemical substance</note> occurs when the water is drawn from the earth, and when one puts the water back on the earth until the earth rots and becomes clean. When the Philosophers saw that the water decreased and the earth increased, they said that it was ceration <note>ceration: from "cera" (wax); the process of softening a substance to a wax-like state</note>. When everything has been made into earth, they said that it was congelation <note>congelation: congealing or solidifying</note>. And when the matter becomes white, they said that this was calcination <note>calcination: heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder or ash</note>. *The Monk, from a manuscript, p. 21.*

### CHAPTER VI.
P iiij

<margin>Desiderabilis <note>Original: "Defiderable"; likely referring to the alchemical treatise "Desiderabilis," a common source in 16th-century compendiums.</note></margin>
Grind <note>original: "Triture"; in alchemy, this refers to breaking down matter, here achieved through heat rather than physical force</note> with fire, not with hands, for first the water tries to dissolve the earth so that it might be of a more subtle <note>subtle: refined, thin, or purified to a gaseous/spiritual state</note> nature than it is; secondly, the earth coagulates the water to the end that it might sustain the fire with it, and this is the dissolution of the body and the coagulation of the spirit. *Desiderabilis, p. 23.*

The solution of the body is the foundation of the Art <note>the Art: Alchemy, often called the "Sacred Art" or "Great Art"</note>, and it is the reduction into water; and from the reduction into water, a reduction into earth is made, putting nothing foreign in, but only taking away the superfluous. *The same author, p. 87.*

The digested spirit is drawn from bodies by the crude spirit. *The same author, p. 264.*

Dissolution engenders blackness, reduction whiteness, fixation yellowness <note>original: "citrinité"; the "citrinitas" stage of the Great Work, occurring between the white and red stages</note>, and inceration <note>inceration: the process of softening a substance until it has a wax-like consistency</note> redness; blackness is the earth, whiteness is the water, yellow or citrine is the air, and redness is the fire. *The same author, p. 269.*

<margin>Richard <note>likely Richardus Anglicus, a celebrated 13th-century alchemist</note></margin>
Art imitates nature, not that it makes a new nature, but rather it refines its virtue; Art therefore begins to profit and advance where nature has failed, uncovering and manifesting the subtlety hidden in the thing. *Richard, chapter 1.*

# CHAPTER VI.

### Scholium. <note>A scholium is an explanatory note or commentary intended to clarify a preceding text.</note>

<margin>Five operations.</margin>
All the operations which are described by the chemical philosophers <note>The "philosophes chymiques" or alchemists.</note> as necessary to this divine work <note>The *Magnum Opus*, the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> can be placed into five classes or orders. In the first, we place commixtion, complection, circondation, composition, and amalgamation; and we shall truly say that all these five are but one, namely the **amalgam** <note>A mixture of a metal with mercury; here it refers to the initial union of the "sol" and "luna" or the formal and material principles.</note>. This amalgam must then be cooked, mortified, burned, calcined, ground, corrupted, digested, dissolved, roasted, and blackened; and all these ten are also but one operation, which is **blackness** <note>Known as the *nigredo* stage, representing the death and putrefaction of the matter.</note>. This blackness must be separated, distilled, and extracted, dividing the dissolved part from the whole; and these four are also but one, namely separating and gathering the blackness, which is the dissolved part of the matter, from the undissolved. This matter must then be revivified, melted, added to, pastured, nourished, submerged, given entry <note>The term "ingrez" or ingress refers to the power of the alchemical medicine to penetrate and transform base metals.</note>, cooled, incerated <note>The process of "inceration" brings the substance to a soft, wax-like state.</note>, reduced, conjoined, impregnated, washed, buried <note>Inhumation: placing the vessel in a warm environment, like a dung heap or sand bath, to maintain gentle heat.</note>, cleansed, congealed, coagulated, augmented, and multiplied for the first time, whitened for the first time, rubified <note>Turned red, the final color of the work.</note> for the first time, dried, watered, moistened, and imbibed; and all these twenty-five are but one, namely **watering and drying**. This desiccation <note>Drying.</note> being done, and the white or red being obtained, it must be fixed, married, fermented, descended, ascended, whitened for the second time, reddened for the second time, made of the nature of fire and very red for the first time, and sublimated for

-># CHEMICAL HARMONY<-

<meta>catchword: digestion</meta>

...for the third time. This being done, if the matter is not fluid enough—that is to say, quickly melting in the fire—one proceeds to ceration <note>The process of "inceration" or ceration brings a substance to a soft, wax-like state, similar to melting wax, to help it flow and combine.</note>. Now, all these terms for operations are stated and noted by their authors, but are poorly understood by those seekers who deceive themselves; some imagine a single specific operation, others imagine several, and consequently believe they need several vessels, furnaces, fires, and a variety of drugs. Yet, if these people possessed good judgment, they would examine the true meaning of these words carefully.

For example, in "commixtion" <note>The act of mixing ingredients.</note> there is more than one matter; if there is more than one matter, the ingredients of this composition must embrace each other, which is understood as "complexion"; this embrace is surrounded by something which is called "circondation" <note>From the Latin *circundare*, meaning to encompass or surround the matter within a vessel or a layer.</note>; in this circondation the composition is formed, and for this composition "amalgamation" necessarily occurs, which is the softening of hard matters. As these matters soften and yield, they dissolve and cast out their seed or "sulphur" <term>Sulphur: In alchemical theory, this is the active, masculine, or combustible principle that gives form and color to the matter.</term> into a black matter, such as was described above. Once this has been gathered, it must be cooked; during this cooking, it takes on a black color, which is called "dead" or "mortified." This mortification is called "combustion"; in this combustion, the matter is said to be "calcined," because lime <note>Original: *chaux*. Calcination involves heating a substance until it is reduced to a fine powder, or "calx," similar to quicklime.</note> is a subtle matter; this subtlety is called "triturated" <note>Ground or pulverized into an extremely fine state.</note>; this trituration is achieved through "corruption" (for no new form can arise in a matter without the loss and corruption of its first form); this corruption cannot take place without digestion <note>The process of slow, gentle heating, similar to how food is broken down in the stomach.</note>.

### CHAPTER VI.

...digestion and cooking. This digestion cannot be accomplished without the dissolution of the first form; in this dissolution, the matter is roasted, and this roasting gradually produces a **blackening**. Once this blackness has been gathered in the desired quantity, it is separated from the superfluous, which is the excess amount of either the mineral water or the body from which it emerged. Thus, what is separated is removed from its dregs. Now, in distillation, the subtle is separated and extracted, or drawn from the thick, and the vapor—which is the matter dissolved from that which is not—is divided from it. 

This black and pure matter, having been separated from the whole, must then be revived because it was dead, and rendered fusible because it was dry, by adding the "meat" <note>Alchemical texts often use metaphors of food to describe the addition of fresh material to the mixture.</note> called <term>cibation</term> <term>Cibation: From the Latin 'cibus' (food); the process of feeding the dry matter with liquid to sustain its growth.</term>, and the nourishment, which is the mercury that is spread over it. This mercury hides itself within this blackness, a step called <term>submersion</term> or **submerging**. Because it penetrates easily, it is called <term>ingression</term>. Because the mercury or the water moistens this hot and dry matter, it is called <term>refrigeration</term> <note>Literally "cooling," referring to the tempering of the "dry heat" of the blackened matter.</note>. Because through this refrigeration the matter becomes liquid and can be spread upon the hand like wax, it is called <term>inceration</term> <note>The process of bringing a substance to a waxy consistency.</note>. This inceration is also called <term>reduction</term> <note>original: "reductio"</note> <term>Reduction: In this context, the act of leading the matter back from a dry, "dead" state to a moist, "living" state.</term>, namely the change from hot and dry into cold and moist. 

In this reduction, the **conjunction** of the water with the black powder takes place; and because the powder grows during this conjunction, it is called <term>conception</term>. Because the black matter then begins to change color, it is said **to wash itself**; and because the mercury is no longer seen,

### CHAPTER VI.

...so much so that under Louis XI, in the year 1465, the gold crown <note>original: "l'escu d'or"</note> was worth 26 shillings 6 pence apiece, as noted on folio 85. ...it is said to be buried <note>original: *inhumer*; the process of "inhumation" where the matter is placed in a vessel to undergo a symbolic death and decay.</note>, and in burying itself it encloses within itself or chases away the blackness; it is then said to be purified <note>original: *mondifier*; to cleanse the matter of its impurities.</note>. And because this mercury does not flow, it is said to be congealed, coagulated, augmented, and multiplied for the first time; for one does not cease adding new mercury to that which is dried and reduced to powder, until the whole is white with the first whiteness. This whiteness, through the continuation of the fire, turns red with the first redness, which is then dried again and moistened again through soaking <term>Imbibition: The process of adding liquid (mercury) to a solid matter to soften it.</term> and sprinkling <term>Irroration: A gentle moistening or "dewing" of the alchemical matter.</term> to join it with its leaven <note>original: *levain*; a substance—usually gold or silver—added to the alchemical mixture to "ferment" it and determine its final state.</note>, which is silver for the white [work], or gold for the yellow, which is called fixation, marriage, fermentation, or descent. 

This is because this matter, which was white or red, becomes black again, then, taking up its white or red color again, it is said to "mount" or ascend. Then this whiteness or redness is called the "second," and the brilliant redness, which darkens into a deep brown-red like burnt crimson blood, is called the "first ignition." And because this redness appeared three times—once without leaven, the second time with leaven, and this third time through the leaven given several times—it is called the "third sublimation," which is to say, rendered excellent for the third time. 

It is in this way, then, that one must understand the good authors, and not imagine fantasies that never were and never shall be. Bodies are not nourished, but only their seeds within themselves through the cooking of the fire, regulated in various ways; for even their bodies are nothing but the food for their seed. It is true that the bodies are changed, altered, and reduced to the nature of the spermatic germ <term>spermatic germ</term> <note>In alchemy, this is the "vital spark" or essence within a metal or mineral that allows it to grow or transform into gold.</note>, and this germ increases by coagulating, and nourishes itself by expanding, like a child on its mother’s milk. Likewise, the bodies resolve like food and are converted into it; in the same way, the dissolution of bodies occurs when the bodies dissolve. The coagulation of one nature does not occur without the dissolution of the other, nor vice versa; and the form to come cannot exist without the corruption of the former form— <note>This follows the Aristotelian principle that "the corruption of one thing is the generation of another." For the Stone to be born, the base material must first "die" or decompose.</note>

It is an error to believe that the bodies of gold and silver—whether in their natural state, or melted, or reduced to "water" (as some believe) by *aqua regia* <term>aqua regia</term> <note>original: "l'eau regale"; a highly corrosive mixture of acids, literally "royal water," capable of dissolving gold.</note> or *aqua fortis* <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>original: "l'eau forte"; nitric acid, used by alchemists to dissolve and test silver.</note>, or filed into dust, or passed through the "beak" of the alembic <term>alembic</term> <note>A classic distillation vessel; the "beak" is the downward-pointing tube through which distilled vapors condense and drip.</note>—can be nourished, increased, or multiplied in quantity or quality, nor even in permanent color by any forced artifice <note>original: "tire poil," an idiom suggesting a superficial or unnatural method that "pulls" at the matter without changing its essence.</note>. But if this germ <note>The "germ" or "seed" is the living essence of the metal that allows for its growth and multiplication.</note> is extracted, as has been stated previously, it can be nourished and raised to a very high degree. # CHAPTER VII.

...seed, increased, coagulated, nourished, and expanded, loses its nature and is dissolved in such a way that it can never again be gold or silver, just as eaten food can never again be food, but becomes something else that is no longer food in the stomach, but is nourishment for all the other parts of the body. For this food often loses the nature it takes on in every place, both during its stay and its passage, insofar as a new form cannot arrive unless the preceding one is lost. However, one must understand and carefully observe that this <margin>Note.</margin> seed, once whitened or reddened, <note>The "whitened" or "reddened" seed refers to the two main stages of the Alchemical Stone: the White Work (turning metals to silver) and the Red Work (turning them to gold).</note> does not "eat" its own body—that is to say, it must not be joined to gold or silver in its physical body except during the fermentation, <term>fermentation</term> <note>In alchemy, fermentation is the final stage where the Stone is joined with a small amount of pure gold or silver to give it a specific "direction" or "flavor" for transmutation.</note> which will be discussed in its proper place.

But here is a significant warning: <margin>Note. Warning.</margin> every time this black matter is "imbibed" <note>To "imbibe" means to repeatedly soak a dry substance with liquid until it is saturated, a process compared to a plant drinking water.</note> on the porphyry <note>original: "porphyre." Yet, within a short time, this whiteness is swallowed up or hidden by the blackness. Finally, however, the water greatly surmounting the earth—by about a fiftieth part, more or less—it begins to demonstrate its power. ->Scholium<-
<note>A scholium is a scholarly commentary or explanatory note used to clarify a specific passage in a text.</note>

"Earth" is understood by Authors in two ways: either during the first composition, for it contains its "son," which is <term>sulfur|one of the primary alchemical principles, representing the active, masculine, and combustible force</term>, within itself, and consequently the four elements, which are black for earth, white for water, yellow for air, and red for fire; in the second way, this earth is simply the blackness, the sulfur, or the "seed," as one might call it, within which blackness the white, yellow, and red are hidden. 

However, in this text, the first way is intended: this "son," which is the blackness, will be nourished by the <term>mercury|the fluid, transformative spirit used to wash and "feed" the solid matter</term> which is its first substance, soaking it and drying it over a slow fire. This must be done not just four times, but until the matter becomes and remains white. One should not be distracted by the "twenty or thirty days" <note>referring to the specific timeframes mentioned for each soaking on the previous page</note>, for the "blood" is consumed according to the strength of the "child" <note>In alchemical allegory, the "child" is the developing Stone, and its "blood" represents the vital energy or moisture it consumes as it matures</note>. It is a true thing that sometimes the drying takes much longer to complete; if one does not wait patiently until the whole has become an <term>impalpable powder|original: "poudre impalpable"; a dust so fine its grains cannot be felt by touch</term>, one is in danger of losing everything: the rest.

The black matter is called "dead" for two reasons: one because, remaining always black, it cannot return to the metals the splendor and the <term>fixation|original: "fixation"; the state where a substance becomes non-volatile and resistant to fire</term> that we seek, and for this reason it is called dead; the other is because of its black color, which is <term>hieroglyphic|a symbolic or sacred representation</term> of death, for dead bodies eventually become black. ->Scholium.<-
<note>A scholium is an explanatory note or commentary on a text.</note>

Let us repeat, although very often, that the first stage of our operations is the dissolution of the bodies; the second is the <term>beheading of the crow|a symbolic name for the stage of "nigredo" or blackness, signifying the death and decomposition of the material</term> or the collection of the dissolved matter or black matter; the third is the washing or nutrition of this dissolved matter with the water that Aristotle calls <term>inceration|the process of softening a substance by gradually adding liquid until it has the consistency of wax</term>, inasmuch as in this operation the matter becomes easy to melt like wax. Now, to show that there is no fixed weight for the water, he says that one must continue this operation until the earth wants no more of it—that is to say, until it becomes white. For when one author says fifty times, another ten, another more, and another less, these are finite numbers used to represent an indefinite process. Previously we spoke of the toad, and the error that many fall into when they take a literal animal toad, and having filled its belly (while still alive) with quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, they place it inside a vessel closed as tightly as they can, and then in or on a fire for some time; which time having passed, and the vessel having cooled and been opened, they find the toad turned to ash...

The compound is the **blackness**, made and drawn out in the form of a seed from the dissolved **Sun** <term>Sun|In alchemical texts, the Sun represents gold, the masculine principle of the Work</term> and **Moon** <term>Moon|The Moon represents silver, the feminine principle of the Work</term>; and in this **divine water** is the **mercury**. But why, he asks, does he say that it does not allow the bodies to break, seeing as every composition of metals in which mercury is most abundant—as it is in this one—is fragile? Could it be to demonstrate the perfection of this work above all others, and to forestall any doubt that might be raised, especially by those who have used **mercurial congelations**? <note>Fixed or solidified states of mercury which were often criticized as being "dead" or brittle in comparison to the "living" philosophical mercury.</note> We could provide other reasons for this, but for now, we content ourselves with these. 

Now, what he previously called the "compound," he now calls the **Art** <note>The "Art" refers to the Great Work of alchemy itself.</note>, then the **earth**, then the **seed**. He exhorts the artist to prudence, so as not to give it too much water at once because of the inconveniences already described; for a child coming out of its mother’s womb has neither the stomach nor the strength to contain, retain, and **cook** <note>original: "cuire". In alchemy, "cooking" or digestion refers to the maturation of the matter through steady, gentle heat.</note> all the milk it suckles and sucks. This it will be able to do some time later, after it has become accustomed to such nourishment. Therefore, one must take great care in this operation, in which lies the knot and secret of the entire affair, inasmuch as there is more artifice required in **whitening** than in **blackening**, **yellowing**, and **reddening**—this operation demanding both industry and patience.

->*Scholium.*<-
<note>A scholium is an explanatory commentary or note intended to clarify a specific passage in a text.</note>

We have stated previously that our "black" is named by many as "fire"; this author understands it so, saying: "make peace between the water and the fire." It follows then that the "little fire" is not common fire, or that this fire which must be pacified with the water is something else entirely. Rather, the spirit, the mercury, the water, the milk, the vile, the burning water, and the **azoth** <term>azoth|The essential agent of transformation, often called the "mercury of the philosophers."</term> are the same thing; and the fire, the body, the **dragon** <term>dragon|A symbol for the "unfixed" or volatile matter that must be tamed or "killed" to reach stability.</term>, the **stone** <term>stone|The Philosophers' Stone in its various stages of development.</term>, the **sulfur** <term>sulfur|The active, solar, or masculine principle in the chemical marriage.</term>, the precious <note>original: 'cher'; referring to the noble or refined portion of the matter, as opposed to the 'vile'.</note>, and the earth are the same thing—namely, the "black." These two must be united so thoroughly that any separation into different parts and properties becomes impossible.

Just as in the first composition of this **Work** <note>The *Magnum Opus* or Great Work of alchemy.</note>, nothing foreign to its nature enters into it, likewise nothing multiplies it that is not of its original disposition; and this Work does not "eat," because it is not a **vegetable** <note>The author distinguishes between biological life, which grows by consuming food, and the "mineral life" of the Stone.</note>. ### Scholium.

We have said before that no one can precisely mark the quantity of milk necessary for a child to strengthen it until it can walk, nor even the amount we need to satisfy ourselves at a meal—we mean by weight or certain measure. Likewise, no one can state the absolute quantity of water necessary to whiten our **moor** <note>original: "more". In alchemical allegory, the "Moor" or "Ethiopian" represents the matter during the *nigredo* (black) stage, which must be "washed" or "whitened" to reach the next stage of the Great Work.</note>: soak it then and nourish it continually until it reaches whiteness; then it will be enough, and the earth will be revived by the water and the true **congelation** <term>congelation|The alchemical process of turning a liquid substance into a solid, often interpreted as the fixing of volatile elements.</term> will be achieved.

### CHAPTER VII.

<margin>The Assembly <note>original: "Tourbe," referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, written as a dialogue between philosophers.</note></margin>
I command that the water be not poured all at once, for fear that the **elixir** <term>elixir|Written here as "yſir," a corruption of the Arabic term "al-iksir," referring to the medicinal or transformative substance.</term> be submerged; but pour it little by little, grind it, dry it, and do this often, until it becomes water. *The Assembly, Proverb 42.*

The unchanging intention of the Philosophers, spoken with a single voice, is that the total power consists of uninterrupted moistening and subsequent grinding, and thus one shall reach the end. *The same, Riddle 7.*

Nourish the body, animate it with its own milk—that is to say, with its own water—from which the work was made or begun from the very first. *Exercise 6 on the Assembly.*

### CHAPTER VII.

<margin>Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century scholar often called the "Father of Chemistry." His works were foundational to European alchemy.</note></margin>
The **thickening** <term>inspissation: the process of making a liquid dense or viscous through evaporation or chemical reaction</term> of any moisture does not occur unless first the **refining** <term>exaltation: in alchemy, raising a substance to a higher state of purity or "dignity"</term> of its subtle parts is performed while preserving the coarser parts; and it is necessary that the moist overcomes the dry in the mixture. Since the true mixture of the dry and the moist lies in the balance between the moist and the dry, and the dry and the moist, a pure and balanced homogeneous substance must be made from them, holding the middle ground between hard and soft, and extending when beaten <note>This refers to the substance becoming "malleable," a key characteristic of perfected metal.</note>. *Geber, book 1, chapter 10, On the Sum of Perfection.* <note>original: "de la sommaire perfection," referring to the "Summa perfectionis magisterii," one of the most famous alchemical texts of the Middle Ages.</note>

From the repeated iteration of **soaking** <term>imbibition: the repeated process of adding liquid to a dry substance and allowing it to absorb</term> with **grinding** <term>contrition: the act of pulverizing or reducing a substance to a fine powder</term> and light **roasting** <term>assation: a method of heating a substance, often in its own moisture, to dry it out</term>, the great moisture of the **mercury** <note>In this context, "mercury" refers to the philosophical principle of liquidity and transformation, not necessarily the common metal.</note> is removed; and then you will see this white, more excellent than snow, remaining on the sides of the **aludel** <term>a series of pear-shaped pots or tubes used as condensers in the process of sublimation</term>, etc. *The same book, chapter 45.*

# CHEMICAL HARMONY

<page-num>326</page-num>

to harmonize the writings. Our Author does not indicate to us here the composition at the <term>commencement of the stone</term> <note>This refers to the "First Work," the initial preparation of the raw materials before they are purified.</note>, but only the <term>fixation</term> <note>fixation: the process of stabilizing a volatile substance so that it can endure the heat of a fire without evaporating.</note> of it—that is to say, to make it such that it cannot be spoiled by any way or manner whatsoever. But by what order should one come to such a high achievement, since it would be of no use to us if we had not passed through the thorny path? We must therefore, without frightening ourselves, walk through these paths full of hydras, bushes, and labyrinths, which have been crossed by several rare spirits, and paved by the loss of the ignorant and the overconfident. Let us begin then with our first fire, which is that of the *solution* <term>solution: the chemical process of dissolving a solid into a liquid, often called "dissolving the body."</term> of solid, whole, clean, and raw bodies.

Fire always tends upward, but reaching toward heaven—because it cannot stagnate—it tends toward other things, seeking to amplify and dilate itself everywhere. Inasmuch as it cannot be drawn downward, because its nature recoils from it, in a very easy conduct and natural course, it leads itself from the soul unto life; this is so that through the communion which it has acquired with higher things through the unique life, it passes to the supreme regions, trying to convert to the supreme not only itself, but also everything it can embrace. For the nature of fire, otherwise [known as] heat and dryness, has tempered itself with the nature of heat and humidity; and from this equal temperament <note>temperament: in pre-modern science, this refers to the specific balance of the four qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry).</note> has come the result that the element of fire has tempered itself with the nature of humidity—from which air, and the element of air, is tempered with the nature of <unclear>fi...</unclear> <note>The text is cut off at the margin; likely "fixity" or "froidure" (coldness), referring to the cycle of the four elements.</note>

Libavius confesses in several places in his works that he did not reach the end and completion of the <term>Philosopher’s Stone</term><note>The ultimate goal of alchemy: a substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold and granting eternal life.</note>, but that by the beginning he witnessed, he judged the rest. We mean those who know the "two hidden points"—which are the extraction of the <margin>Two hidden points, and which ones.</margin> <term>redness</term> <note>original: "rouilleure" (rustiness/redness). In alchemy, this often refers to the rubedo stage or the formation of a red oxide.</note> or blackness, and its <term>imbibition</term> <note>imbibition: The process of repeatedly "feeding" or soaking a solid substance with a liquid until it is saturated or transformed.</note>. These people know all the rest, provided they know it either by divine inspiration or by study; for someone might well name these two operations—very troublesome, very difficult, and very hidden—but they will not understand them at all without understanding all the other operations.

Now, our Author says our matter must be spread at the bottom of the vessel, whereupon it is asked whether this <margin>Doubt.</margin> operation refers to the time when it must be "rusted" <note>Referring to the process of oxidation or achieving the red stage.</note>, or the time when this "rust," soaked in its <term>vinegar</term> <note>original: "vinaigre." Likely "Philosophical Vinegar," a potent solvent used to break down the matter.</note>, must be dried. To this we answer that this spreading applies to both the one and <margin>Solution.</margin> the other operation, but more particularly to the second. For in that stage, three-quarters of the vessel must be empty. One must observe through experience that a wet cloth laid out flat dries sooner than one heaped in a pile, and that a quantity of dough spread out is baked sooner than one piled together. ### Scholium. <note>A scholarly commentary or explanatory note added to a text.</note>

**Libavius** <note>Andreas Libavius (1555–1616), a German physician and chemist known for his work "Alchemia," which attempted to organize alchemical knowledge systematically.</note> confesses in several places in his works that he did not reach the end and completion of the **Philosophers' Stone**, but that by the beginning which he saw, he judged the rest; this is what we have said previously, namely, that those who know the beginning of it also know the end. For someone might well speak of these two very troublesome, very difficult, and very hidden operations, yet he will not understand them at all if he does not understand all the other operations. 

Now, says our Author, our matter must be scattered at the bottom of the vessel, upon which it is asked whether this <margin>Doubt.</margin> operation is intended for the time when it is necessary to rust, or for the time when it is necessary to dry this rust soaked in its **vinegar** <note>The "Philosophical Vinegar," a powerful solvent used to dissolve or "wash" the matter.</note>. To which it is answered that this scattering is intended for <margin>Solution.</margin> both the one and the other operation, but more particularly for the second. For in that one, three parts of the vessel must be empty; one must see by experience that a wet cloth which is spread out is dry sooner than one piled up, and that a quantity of dough spread out is cooked sooner than a heap. It is therefore necessary to have a vessel shaped in proportion to the matter...

### Scholium. <note>A scholium is a marginal note or explanatory comment, common in scholarly and scientific texts of the period.</note>

<margin>
<unclear>Compare</unclear>

Many believe, as Augurel <note>Giovanni Aurelio Augurello (1441–1524), an Italian poet and alchemist famous for his work *Chrysopoeia*.</note> says, that the **philosophical work** must never be cooled under penalty of losing all past progress, but Greuerius <note>Jodocus Greverus, a 16th-century author known for his treatise *Secretum*, which focused on the practical steps of the Great Work.</note> clearly shows that they are mistaken. And truly, after some time of nourishment <note>In alchemy, "nourishment" refers to the addition of more matter (the "philosophical milk") to the substance in the vessel to sustain its growth or chemical reactions.</note> having been interrupted for some years, and consequently the **vessel** and **matter** having been removed from the fire, the work took up new nourishment very well and very easily; it had lost nothing but time. The strength of it was in no way diminished because the vessel was very well sealed, so that nothing could enter or leave it. And in fact, if a steady and continuous fire were required, how could that be possible when, in order to dissolve, congeal, and fix, one must change both the vessel and the fire? For there is an operation in which the fire must be at such a degree that it reddens the bottom of the vessel containing the one where the matter is held <note>This describes a sand-bath or a double-vessel setup where an outer container is heated to a glow to provide intense but indirect heat to the inner retort.</note>, and this degree lasts no more than one or two hours—we mean during the first operation, for toward the end it lasts longer. Regarding the two fires of which Alanus <note>Alanus de Insulis, mentioned on the previous page.</note> speaks, he explains them clearly enough, but where he says that the **mineral** is not taken from the matter, he means from the matter that the Philosophers have drawn from the two substances; nor even is it drawn from the same mine from which **gold** and **silver** are drawn, for **mercury** has a particular mine <note>The author is distinguishing between common metals found in the earth and the "Philosophical Mercury," which alchemists believed came from a more fundamental source.</note>.

There are four fires which have the power to burn: the natural fire coagulates, the non-natural fire dissolves, the fire against nature corrupts, and the elemental fire provides the first heat and first movement. <note>These "four fires" represent different stages or qualities of heat in the laboratory, ranging from literal physical flame to the internal "vital heat" of the materials.</note> From these, a successive order is seen, for the second fire is moved by the first, the third by the second, and the fourth by the third and by the first, in such a way that one is the agent and the other the patient; thus one acts as the agent while the other is the patient in various ways. <note>The terms "agent" and "patient" are Aristotelian concepts: the agent is the active force that causes change, while the patient is the matter being acted upon.</note> *Atalanta Fugiens, p. 78.* <note>original: "Atalante fuyante"; referring to the famous emblem book by Michael Maier (1617) which used Greek myths as alchemical allegories.</note>

<margin>Artephius</margin> <note>Artephius (c. 1150) was a legendary alchemical author to whom several influential medieval texts were attributed.</note>
<insert>280 / 416</insert>
Artephius maintains that the fire called "mineral"—which is steady, continuous, non-vaporous (unless excessively excited), participating in the nature of sulfur, taken from a source other than the matter itself, ruining everything, dissolving, congealing, and calcining—is artificially discovered. This fire shortens the process without great expense. This vaporous moisture—which digests, alters, penetrates, and is subtle, airy, non-violent, non-burning, surrounding, containing, and unique—and as a corollary is hot, dry, moist, and cold—should be understood as three fires. These are: the lamp fire, which is shining and burning; the fire of ashes, upon which the vessel is placed; and the third is our water, which is also called "against nature." <note>The "fire against nature" (*ignis contra naturam*) is a famous alchemical paradox; it refers to a chemical solvent or "mercurial water" that acts like fire by dissolving solids, even though it is a liquid.</note> Join these three fires together, and you will infallibly achieve the Work of the Philosophers, since you understand their fire.

<meta>This page transitions from the general discussion of alchemical fires to a specific practical commentary (scholium) on the purification of matter. It continues the instructions for the "Great Work," moving into the preparation of the base material known as "latten" or the "raven’s head."</meta>

<page-num>350</page-num>

<header>CHEMICAL HARMONY</header>

->*Scholium.*<-

Take the latten, says our author—that is to say, the rust or the "raven's head" and its feathers—and sift it well. <note>The "raven’s head" (*caput corvi*) is a traditional alchemical term for the *nigredo* or black stage of the process, representing the death and putrefaction of the base matter.</note> That is to say, separate it so industriously, whether with a sieve or with the wing of a feather, that no part of either the flesh or the bones, or any other part of the body remains there. Otherwise, whatever remains of the earthly and coarse will prevent the subtle and spiritual from reaching the desired effect. Now, this material thus cleaned—which will be a blackish red or a blackish gray—shall be placed in a suitable vessel with our very well rectified water of life in a tenfold quantity, <note>original: "eau de vie"; in alchemical practice, this refers to a potent distilled solvent or "mercurial water," rather than common brandy.</note> over a fire convenient for cooking. Then these two things, uniting, will rise, bubble up, and produce something like a grease or sticky foam. Once this has cooled, it must be properly separated from its surplus, which shall be reserved to serve several more times. This foam is properly the **drool of Cerberus** (the three-headed dog, guardian of the gates of hell), <margin>*Drool of Cerberus.*</margin> whose venom kills whatever it falls upon. Throw it, then, into a pit and close it very securely, guarding yourself against its smoke, and do not leave the slightest part of it among our water of life. This being done, our <term>latten</term> <note>Latten (*laton*) here refers to the impure metallic body that must be "whitened" or purified through the alchemical process.</note> being positioned as it should, will dry out and reduce first into a discontinuous matter, like a paste, and then, being dried, into an impalpable powder—

# CHAPTER IX.

—namely <term>matrass: a long-necked glass chemical flask, also known as a bolt-head</term> matrasses, consider carefully what we tell you: if your <term>orpiment: a deep orange-yellow arsenic sulfide mineral used as a pigment and in alchemical experiments</term> orpiment, your arsenic, and your devouring water <term>devouring water: a corrosive alchemical solvent, such as a strong acid, used to break down metallic substances</term> weigh ten ounces, your vessel can and must contain thirty, in which you will petrify, dissolve, rust, and separate the seed, or sulfur, or blackness from its own body. This blackness <note>The *nigredo* or "black work," signifying the first stage of the Great Work involving the decomposition or "death" of the matter.</note> is sometimes reddish, sometimes grayish, and sometimes blackish; but do not worry about what color it is, for little by little it will blacken enough. 

Take the case that you have one ounce of this blackness; you will put it with a dozen ounces of its devouring water inside a matrass containing about thirty-six ounces, on a boiling fire (but take care at this passage, for it is easy to slip up). By this fire, the dry and the moist will fight, and from the two a paste will be made; and like grease or foam it will float, which, being separated, might weigh two ounces. These you must put inside a matrass containing about six ounces, very well closed, on the proper fire which little by little will reduce this paste to powder. 

This very subtle matter will be put back with its boiling water, as before, which being duly governed will return to a paste, and being removed will be put into another slightly larger vessel, because it will weigh more; and being dried out, it will be returned to a paste. To say it in a word, this will be re-pasted and pulverized until the matter is white <note>The *albedo* or "white work," the second major stage of alchemy, representing purification.</note>; then you shall touch it no more until such time as you see the matter turned red <note>The *rubedo* or "red work," the final stage of the alchemical process resulting in the Philosopher's Stone.</note>.

…and not young men, especially since the impatient young are blinded by the brevity of time, which cannot provide what length of duration gives to the patient elders. For this reason, all the <term>Philosophers: the term used by alchemists to describe themselves and their predecessors in the study of nature</term> exhort one to have patience throughout the duration; he who will not have patience, therefore, should not work at all, for every action has its own movement and set time. Now, the <term>medicine: the Philosopher's Stone or the elixir of transformation</term> is not made in a few days or months, nor in a brief span, seeing as it must be tamed and nourished by the fire for a long time—a feat accomplished only through a great length of time and great dexterity. *From an Epistle, beginning: My Lord <note>original: "Domine mi"</note>, p. 47.*

<margin>Armingand <note>A reference to Armingandus, a medieval authority often cited in alchemical compendiums</note></margin>
Cook and <term>triturate: to grind or pulverize a solid into a fine powder</term>, and do not grow weary of repeating this, for the more you triturate, the more you <term>subtilize: the process of refining a substance until it reaches its most delicate, "subtle," or spiritualized form</term> the coarse parts; for by great <term>assation: a method of dry heating or roasting over a fire</term>, trituration, and long <term>decoction: the process of boiling a substance in a liquid to extract its essence</term>, our <term>bodies: the metallic or mineral substances being transformed</term> are dissolved. Have patience, therefore, because they are of a strong and hard resolution <note>meaning they have a very stable and dense physical structure that resists change</note>; for if you fully understood their natures, you would wait patiently and with joy. He who does not love patience, therefore, should not undertake our <term>work: the "Great Work" (Magnum Opus), the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</term>, for fear that he might ruin himself. *Armingandus, ch. 3.*

Among all the difficulties encountered in this admirable quest, there is not one that distracts researchers as much as the length of time necessary to complete the work; this is what makes them look for some "branches" (as they say) of this tree in some little corner to carry the burden, while they wait until they have the means to set their hand to the "Great Work" (as they call it). They run, therefore—in order to get there sooner—to <term>congelations: the process of solidifying a liquid</term>, <term>fixations: making a volatile substance stable under heat</term>, <term>whitenings: the stage of the work producing silver (albedo)</term>, <term>reddenings: the final stage producing gold (rubedo)</term>, <term>medions: intermediate medicines</term>, and <term>tiercelets: fractional transmutations</term> of ten percent, thirty, forty—some more, some less per cent. ### Scholium <note>original: "Scholie"; a marginal note or explanatory commentary on a text, common in early modern scholarly works</note>

<margin>24. C</margin>
Everything that has happened or must come to pass leaves marks, either of its present arrival, its future arrival, its duration, or its departure—be it swift or slow. However, the cause and the subject are not always known to us, just as flowers signal the coming fruit to us, or the impregnation of females signals the animals to come. In the same way, the black color <term>black color: known as "nigredo," this is the essential first stage of the Great Work, symbolizing the death and decomposition of the substance</term> appearing in our matter signals to us that it is good, well-ruled, and well-governed. 

We are not unaware that many operators <note>practicing alchemists, often called "puffers" if they lacked the philosophical understanding of the art</note> have seen this blackness, but not knowing how to lead and conduct it as they should, they have thrown it away as a useless and excremental thing, seeing and calling it the "filth of mercury" <note>original: "saleté du mercure"; mercury was considered the fundamental metallic principle, but in its raw state, it was thought to contain "leprosy" or impurities that had to be purged</term>. 

But even when told to purify it in whatever manner they might wish, and that once thus purified they should mix it with gold and silver—the one reduced to twenty-four carats <note>the standard for the highest purity of gold</note> and the other to twelve deniers <note>a historical French measure of silver fineness, where 12 deniers represents pure silver</note>—for then one shall come out of the fire yellow and burnished, and the other white and burnished, they preferred to remain in their stubbornness and ignorance, asking what good this blackness is, if not for blackening shoes. 

Oh, ignorant ones! This blackness is the sign, or the true dissolved matter, without which the Philosophers <note>the "Philosophers" refers to the ancient and medieval masters of alchemy whose writings formed the "Hermetic" tradition</note> have never accomplished anything good, nor shall anyone ever do so in this art. It is this blackness which is the principle, element, and foundation of the whole, and to which so much [has been given]...

rents and mother have passed through to reach the <unclear>goal</unclear> of begetting. Now, our said matter <unclear>having</unclear> emerged and been collected, is partly as if <unclear>fixed</unclear> and partly volatile; this latter part vanishing into <unclear>smoke</unclear> over a strong fire and in a crucible <term>crucible: a heat-resistant container for melting metals</term>, and the other part attaching itself there in the form of a varnish spotted with white, shining points, like small grains of silver. All this is without fruit other than finding this thing to be true, of which several Philosophers have written because they have experienced it—and we with them—and of which they say to beware of vitrification <note>vitrification: the process of turning into glass. In alchemy, this was often considered a "dead end" where the matter became fused and useless.</note>.

But if, quite to the contrary of this strong fire, one nourishes this matter little by little with its own milk <term>milk: a metaphorical term for a nourishing solvent or the "mercurial" liquid used to feed the stone</term>, it will increase infinitely as has been said before. And whatever increase or color it may have—be it white, yellow, or red—it can always be sent up in smoke, because it is always volatile, having come from a volatile matter. 

However, when it has taken on the white or red color, and is allied with silver or gold, it will undoubtedly be rendered fixed and permanent against any fire, and more besides in proof: by this we further clarify the passage of him who says that the white stone is made with white mercury and silver, and the red stone with red mercury and with gold. For the black having arrived at the white (our white mercury) will be fermented <term>fermented: the stage where the alchemical "medicine" is joined with a small amount of pure gold or silver to give it "seed" and stability</term> with silver; but being red (which is done by the continuation of the fire), it will be fermented with gold. And that is the truth, without imagining any other fantasy. For

# CHAPTER XII.

**Leaven** or **ferment** is understood and interpreted in various ways by many; some take the black, white, or red powder to be the leaven, while others take it to be silver or gold. But this difficulty should not stop the artist, for what does it matter if we call the leaven—from which one makes bread dough rise—the "paste," or if we say that the flour mixed with water is the leaven? Whether one specifies this word by its power or remains silent, it is enough to know that just as leaven, which is quite sour, makes the flour and water-paste sour when mixed together, so too does this powder make the mercury added to it—little by little and over time in great quantities—black, subtle, and impalpable. 

Nor does it matter if one takes silver or gold as the leaven or ferment; it is enough only to know that the intention of the Philosophers <note>Philosophers: In this context, the author refers to the "Alchemical Philosophers," the historical masters of the Hermetic art whose writings formed the basis of this study.</note> and their doctrine is that this black powder must be nourished with a quantity of mercury until that blackness has disappeared, and whiteness has arrived, and after that, redness <note>These colors refer to the three main stages of the "Great Work": the Nigredo (black), Albedo (white), and Rubedo (red).</note>. 

This black, white, or red matter is called by many "earth," "dirty and filthy body," and "volatile," which must be joined with gold—which some call "leaven," "ferment," "body," "soul," and other names—by means of mercury. This mercury is called by many "gum," "glue," "medium," or "spirit," joining the soul with the body. For indeed, without this mercury—which has nourished the blackness and which shares in the nature of the powder, the silver, and the gold—the union cannot be made only...

->### CHEMICAL HARMONY<-

But it is asked: what is this black, white, and red powder? One responds (within this science) that it is a body or an accidental property without form, since it is still volatile. For after it has been given its fixation through the joining of the Moon <term>Moon: Alchemical symbol for silver, representing the white stage of the Work.</term> for the white, and of the Sun <term>Sun: Alchemical symbol for gold, representing the final red stage.</term> for the red, then it will possess its true form and soul. This is evident because the matter will then subsist and withstand every kind of trial—and with good reason, since it is the form (not the visible and accidental form, but the essential one) which causes things to truly exist. As the Philosophers say, *form gives being to the thing* <note>original Latin: "forma dat esse rei." This is a fundamental Scholastic principle meaning that the "form" or essence of an object is what makes it what it is.</note>. 

Now, if this matter—having been nourished, fermented, and in a word, completed—has the power to purify such a great quantity of impure metals when cast upon them in a very small weight (such as one grain to a thousand, or even more grains, though someone more daring than I may speak of that), we can certainly assure you of this: one ounce of this **raven’s head** <note>The "raven’s head" (*caput corvi*) is a traditional alchemical term for the deep black color that appears during the *Nigredo* stage, signifying the "death" or decomposition of the matter before its rebirth.</note> has reduced fifty ounces of mercury into a blackness like its own before the whiteness appeared. For afterward, it no longer needs to be "nourished" <note>In alchemy, "nourishing" refers to the repeated addition of mercury to the matter to increase its volume or potency.</note>. It is believable that it can achieve much with little weight over a great mass; but if the seeker desires to know the final result, his own patient and assiduous labor will clarify it for him. 

Let us be content to know what we know, and to have seen, by a particular blessing from God, what He has permitted us to see. We swear before Him who still permits us to live that we have spoken and written all the means of obtaining this **admirable treasure** as clearly as anyone we have seen before now.

<summary>The author explains how the alchemical powder gains its "essential form" through the symbolic marriage of Sun and Moon, eventually achieving the power to transmute large quantities of base metal. He concludes with a solemn oath that he has revealed the process as clearly as possible, attributing his success to divine favor.</summary>
<keywords>Fixation, Moon (Silver), Sun (Gold), Essential Form, Raven's Head (Nigredo), Mercury, Projection, Alchemical Treasure</keywords>

### Scholium.

It is commonly said that "common error makes the law," <note>original: *l'erreur commun faict la loy*; a reference to the legal maxim *communis error facit jus*, suggesting that a widely held belief becomes an accepted rule.</note> but I say that the error of the **ignorant** does not dictate the law to the **learned**. The ignorant insist that the **medicine of the Philosophers** <gloss>The Philosopher's Stone or Elixir.</gloss> purifies all **metals**, and as they say, reduces them to **gold**, if the medicine is red, or to **silver**, if it is white. This cannot be—I mean regarding their common medicine and first preparation. For no **natural agent**, acting according to nature, acts beyond its own degree, unless it acts upon a subject that possesses some quality similar to itself, which makes it susceptible to such action. Through this property of the subject and its capacity for being acted upon, the agent imprints and imparts to it all that it can. 

**For example**: a candle lit in a room will illuminate the surrounding air, but the air will not receive more light than is present in the flame of the candle; otherwise, the flame would be acting beyond its degree. However, if one brings a **crystal** near this flame, one will see within it a greater light than that which is in the flame of the candle itself. This happens because of that property or **susceptibility** that the **crystal** has for receiving this light, and not otherwise. The same is true of our **medicine**, from which all imperfect or "dirty" metals cannot receive the pu... <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely intended to be "purity" (pureté) or "power" (puissance).</note>

<vocab>medicine of the Philosophers, metals, gold, silver, natural agent, crystal, flame, susceptibility</vocab>

<summary>This page argues that the Philosopher's Stone does not work indiscriminately on all materials, but requires a "susceptible" subject, using the analogy of a candle flame's interaction with air versus a crystal.</summary>

<margin>
The gold that is eaten <note>original: "L'or qui se mange"; a reference to *Aurum Potabile* or potable gold, a medicinal liquid gold believed to grant longevity.</note>
</margin>

Note that everything that is transmuted into another is no longer what it was before, and through this loss of what it once possessed, it corrupts entirely—experiencing every kind of corruption—in order to become nourishment for another. As Solon remarked at the *Banquet of the Seven Sages* in Plutarch's *Opuscula*: "Every transmutation follows the nature of the transmuting agent, and the transmuting agent does not take on the nature of the thing transmuted." Therefore, if the transmuting agent is volatile and combustible, that which is transmuted will be the same. 

**Pico della Mirandola** <note>Italian Renaissance philosopher (1463–1494) who wrote on the Kabbalah and alchemy.</note> and others note having seen the **projection** performed in several ways; this does not, however, indicate different medicines, but a single one that can be mixed with various materials—such as wax, soap, tallow, **vitriol**, <note>A general term for sulfate minerals, often used as catalysts or solvents in alchemical recipes.</note> and the like—which vanish in the fire. The single medicine then attaches and unites with the molten **metal**, from which it separates the impurity and perfects the rest. By this differing manner of projection, even those most learned in other sciences are deceived by the belief they adopt that there are diversities of ways and means...

[...itself, the earth is the] receptacle of the germ, and the water is the matrix of the seed. *Treatise on Sulfur, page 6.* <note>original: "Traicté du soulphre." This refers to the work of Michael Sendivogius, a famous 17th-century alchemist.</note>

<margin>Aristotle, Book 8 <note>Historical citation error: Aristotle's *On the Generation of Animals* consists of only five books; the author may be citing a later commentary or a different collection.</note> of *On the Generation of Animals*, chapter 8, distinguishes the offspring <note>original: "geniture"</note> or germ from the seed.</margin>
Fire acting against air produces sulfur; air acting against water produces salt; water acting against earth produces mercury; but the earth, finding no other element against which it might act, can produce nothing itself; instead, it retains in its center what the other three have produced, so that there are only three principles <term>three principles: known as the "Tria Prima" (Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt), these were considered by Paracelsian alchemists to be the fundamental components of all matter</term> for which the earth remains both matrix and nurse. *The same [author], page 40.*

The body is the earth, the spirit is the water, and the soul is the fire (or the sulfur of gold). The spirit increases only the quantity of the body, but the soul—or the sulfur, or the fire—increases its virtue <term>virtue: the inherent medicinal or transformative power of a substance</term>. But since there is more spirit (that is, water) by weight than fire, the spirit exalts itself and oppresses the fire, drawing it to itself, so that each of these two increases in virtue, and the earth—which is the medium or middle ground between them—grows in weight. *The same [author], page 43.*

This mercury carries its own sulfur and cannot exist without it; indeed, it is often called sulfur itself. This sulfur is the **fiery virtue** <term>virtue: the inherent power or active property of a substance</term> hidden within, which makes this mercury dry and powdered. When this powder is moistened by its own water, it is turned into something like a white foam floating upon the water. However, it must be noted that Mercury is understood in two ways (or for two things) by the Philosophers: namely, as a **volatile matter** in fire, and as a **fixed matter** that remains within it. If the diligent student carefully considers the passages of good authors, they will easily recognize the reason for the variety of so many names. For now, let us be content to learn...

# CHAPTER XVII.

<meta>Signature: Ee iiij</meta>

that common **quicksilver** <term>quicksilver: common liquid mercury, which alchemists distinguished from the "mercury of the philosophers" needed for their work</term> is not at all that of the Philosophers, any more than common sulfur is. We readily admit that ours cannot appear except through the help of the common sort; however, we also say that the common sort abandons ours as soon as it has emerged from its two bodies, with which it must afterwards be joined. As for common sulfur, it has no access nor entry into our matter; ours being only the **hot, dry, and drying virtue** <note>In the theory of the four humors/elements, sulfur was associated with heat and dryness, acting as the "masculine" or active principle that "fixes" the mercury.</note>, which emerges equally from the components along with our mercury—of which we have previously discussed at great length.

If it is true, the curious but not subtle seeker will say, that one must pay no regard either to the stars, nor to the time, nor to the hours, then why is it that the **Philosophers** <note>In this context, "Philosophers" refers specifically to the "Adepts" or masters of alchemy.</note> tell us to begin working in the month of March? Why should we wait for the conjunction of **Mercury** with **Saturn**, why that of the said **Mercury** with **Mars**, then with **Jupiter**, then with the **Moon**, then with the **Sun**, without which nothing will be accomplished? Certainly, just as the season in the month of March is temperate, and the air there is neither too hot, nor too cold, nor too dry, nor too humid, so too is it desired that at the beginning, the heat by which the <term>cooking: the process of heating the matter in a sealed vessel over a long period.</term>, putrefaction, or corrosion of our <term>chaos: the "Materia Prima" or raw, unrefined substance the alchemist begins with.</term> or mixture must be performed, should be gentle. This is so that through this gentleness, the whole may embrace and unite itself better and more easily; for if the heat were too great, the bond, glue, paste, and gum which must unite the male and the female <note>The "male" and "female" represent the active (sulfur) and passive (mercury) principles of matter which must be joined.</note> would vanish, and the two bodies would remain dry without any production, neither of blackness, nor of branchings, <note>referring to "dendritic" growth, where crystals form patterns resembling tree branches inside the glass vessel.</note> nor of any other color. Indeed, it is a true thing that our **sea water**—whose heart cannot support an overly violent heat without falling into a fever—would die, and by its death, our entire work would be ruined. Let the heat of the season in this month, therefore, serve as a model for the conduct of our work, and thus it will serve—

# CHAPTER XVII.

...[we] will speak of the conduct and likeness of the other months and seasons of the year. When it comes to the conjunctions of the planets, that of **Mercury** with **Saturn** is when blackness appears on the matter due to the <term>melancholic humor: one of the four bodily humors, associated here with the "Nigredo" or black stage of alchemy.</term>. That with **Mars** is the gray color—though others say it is the reddish-yellow color—due to the yellow <term>choler: or bile, representing a stage of "cooking" or heat.</term> which is slightly cooked. That of **Jupiter** is the first whiteness. That of the **Moon** is the great whiteness, due to the <term>phlegm: the cool, moist humor associated with the "Albedo" or white stage.</term>. And that of the **Sun** is due to the great redness and the fire or blood. That of **Venus** occurs when love or the heating takes place between the two substances.

It is in this fashion that we must understand the sayings of the **Philosophers**, both ancient and modern. This truth means that we do not need to expand further upon the discourse of these celestial sciences, since they are not necessary to us in this work, any more than is an understanding of all the enigmas. To untie those riddles, one would sooner have to bring the authors who proposed them back to life than to try to explain and interpret them. 

For who is the geometer who can <term>square the circle: a famous mathematical problem of constructing a square with the same area as a circle, used here to represent the "impossible" task of alchemical transformation.</term>, reduce this square into a triangle, this triangle into a line, and this line into a point (which is indivisible), which contains as much within itself as it did while it was a line, a triangle, a quadrangle, or a round circle? Would one not say that this is entirely impossible? And yet the chemical **Philosopher** performs this through the accomplishment of this art, and without this, he understands nothing of it; a man of the...

It is this which moved the **Alchemists** to name lead **Saturn**, gold the **Sun**, and silver the **Moon**. However, they differ from the **Astrologers**, who assign copper to **Jupiter**, while the Alchemists give him tin; to **Venus**, the Astrologers give tin, whereas the Alchemists give her copper. <note>This reversal of planetary associations for tin and copper was a common point of divergence between celestial astrology and terrestrial alchemy in the 17th century.</note> Both, however, assign iron and sulfur to **Mars**, and quicksilver to **Mercury**. 

If the knowledge of what is commonly called the **Philosophers' Stone** <note>original: "pierre des Philosophes"</note> could be acquired through debate, it would be somewhat easy to obtain; but those who have grasped it by the right end have only cared to write of it to prove that it is real, and to provide the means for curious seekers to gain that same knowledge. They describe it through riddles, similes, or examples. 

Many others, however, acting out of ostentation after having consumed their own means and those of others in fantasies—furnaces, vessels, fires, and mineral, animal, and vegetable drugs—amuse themselves without understanding the true meaning of the authors. They attempt to draw their principle from volatile and combustible materials, not believing that "each produces its like," <note>A fundamental alchemical maxim: *ours produces ours*. ### CHAPTER XVII,

...principle <note>Continuing from the previous page: "Just as a tree whose principle..."</note> is drawn from a combustible thing, its product cannot be stable. In the **expurgatory index** <note>original: "indice expurgatoire"; a curated list intended to separate reliable texts from fraudulent or "cluttered" ones.</note> which will soon see the light of day, God willing, the good authors will be distinguished from the scribblers. I speak of those of whom we have had knowledge, for it is very difficult to have seen or known all the books that have treated this subject until now; nor should one believe that all books bearing the name of an author were actually composed by him. 

Now, I maintain that no one can understand fundamentally, nor distinguish a good author from a bad one, if he has not seen and does not know very well how to **extract his fire** without destroying the matter, and how to **nourish it**. For if these two points are unknown, all the rest is as well. The understanding of these two points may have been easier for certain other more refined spirits than for **David Laigneau**, who spent twenty-two years in this research before becoming Physician to the King, and who composed and arranged his **Harmony** <note>Referring to Laigneau’s work, *Harmonie Chimique* (1636), which attempted to reconcile the conflicting statements of various alchemists.</note> not upon the model of this aforementioned "thorny and brushy bundle" <note>original: "fagot brossailleux, & espineux"; a disparaging metaphor for a poorly constructed or confusing book.</note>—which, along with its author (whom I do not believe to be the one whose name it bears), deserves nothing but the fire. 

Let us not, therefore, be carried away by the **puffers** <term>souffleurs: a derogatory term for amateur or fraudulent alchemists who focused on the physical bellows (blowers) rather than the philosophical theory.</term> and deceivers; let us hold fast to the truth, for which God will show us the way and grant us possession—not only of this treasure <note>The Philosophers' Stone.</note>, if He deems it necessary for us, but of the heavenly one through the intercession of our Lord **Jesus Christ**, our only Savior and Redeemer, to whom with the Father and the Holy Spirit be praise, honor, and blessing forever and ever. **Amen**.

<summary>David Laigneau reflects on his twenty-two years of alchemical study, warning readers against fraudulent texts and "puffers" while emphasizing that true chemical understanding requires mastery of "fire." The text concludes with a prayer, situating the search for the Philosophers' Stone within a framework of Christian devotion.</summary>

# THE PRINTER TO THE Reader.

Having recovered some papers already aged by time, and examining them with several of my friends who are expert in this **mystical science** <note>original: "science mystique"; referring here to alchemy and the hermetic arts.</note>, they found it appropriate to offer to the **studious seeker** <note>original: "curieux studieux"; a common 17th-century term for a dedicated student of natural philosophy and the hidden arts.</note> the following pieces, chosen from among them. As these are in no way contrary to the preceding treatise, enjoy them, therefore, to your heart's content.

The physician <note>Aesculapius, the Greco-Roman god of medicine, here representing the Alchemist who guides the chemical transformation.</note> came to visit him, and ordered for him a bath composed of certain drugs cleansed of their sandy impurities. <margin>*Nutrition and desiccation*</margin> In this bath, before a fire, Apollo <note>Apollo is the alchemical symbol for Gold.</note> was anointed several times, being dried as many times as he was rubbed; then he was placed back into a bath made of the dregs of Bacchus <note>original: "excrements de Bacchus." This refers to wine lees, tartar, or perhaps a strong vinegar used as a solvent in the alchemical process.</note> for a certain space of time. Apollo diminished and melted in this bath, like snow in the Sun, and in all the water of the bath it seemed that his substance was dissipated. Aesculapius drained the bathwater, which he set aside, and gave him more of the same, bathing him thus many times, and almost as often as he had rubbed, washed, and dried him with the other. Afterward, to warm him again, he applied a small fire to the waters he had drawn from the bath, before which the moisture <margin>*yellow.* <note>The original "laune" is likely a variant or misspelling of "jaune" (yellow), referring to the "Citrinitas" or yellowing stage of the alchemical work.</note></margin> that made Apollo all wet evaporated; and being dry, he still seemed to have been rendered more feeble by all these baths, ointments, and washings. -># CHEMICAL HARMONY<-

I saw him present himself before him; he gave to <term>Aesculapius<note>The Greco-Roman god of medicine and healing, often used in alchemy to represent the curative power of the Work.</note></term> the most beautiful and most precious thing that was within him, which he suddenly gave to <term>Apollo<note>In alchemical symbolism, Apollo represents the Sun, the spirit of Gold, or the perfected state of matter.</note></term> to swallow. After this intake, Apollo seemed to be resuscitated, regaining a complexion wonderfully lively and beautiful, with such a 
<margin>*Projection*<note>The final stage of the alchemical Great Work, where the 'Philosopher's Stone' or medicine is cast upon base metals to transform them, or used to heal the body.</note></margin> fullness of life that, by communicating his state to the sick and the decrepit, he restores them to a better condition than they had ever been in before.

<summary>This passage uses the mythological figures of Aesculapius and Apollo to describe the final stage of the alchemical process, where a "precious" substance grants perfect vitality. This perfected state, known as Projection, acts as a universal medicine that can rejuvenate the sick and the elderly.</summary>
<keywords>Alchemy, Aesculapius, Apollo, Projection, healing, vitality, transmutation, Great Work</keywords>

### Royal Privilege.

Louis, by the grace of God King of France & of Navarre, To our beloved and faithful Councilors holding our Courts of Parliaments, Masters of Requests in ordinary of our Household, Bailiffs, Seneschals, Provosts, their Lieutenants, and our other Justices and Officers whom it may concern, Greetings: Our dear and well-beloved Melchior Mondiere <note>A prominent 17th-century Parisian bookseller and printer located on the Rue Saint-Jacques, known for publishing scientific and esoteric works.</note>, Merchant Bookseller and Printer of our City of Paris, has caused to be told and shown to Us that he has recovered a Book entitled *Mystical Harmony or the agreement of the Chemical Philosophers with the Scholia on the most difficult passages of the Authors cited therein, etc.* <note>The "Chemical Philosophers" refers to alchemists, and "Scholia" are explanatory comments or annotations on a primary text.</note> composed by **David Laigneau** <term>Physician-in-ordinary</term> <note>original: "Medecin ordinaire." This title indicates that Laigneau was part of the King's regular medical staff, a position of significant professional status.</note>, which he desires to print or have printed, sell, and distribute; for this purpose, he has petitioned us to grant him our required and necessary letters, desiring to treat him favorably: **FOR THESE CAUSES**, we have permitted and do permit him by these presents to print or have printed, sell or have sold during the term of twelve years the said Book, counting from the day that it shall be finished being printed for the first time, in such form, volume, and characters as shall seem good to him, during which time we make very express inhibitions and prohibitions to all persons from printing it, having it printed, selling, or distributing it under <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword "sous" (under) indicates the beginning of the legal penalties for copyright infringement on the following page.</note>

<summary>This page presents the official Royal Privilege granted by King Louis XIII to the printer Melchior Mondière for David Laigneau's alchemical treatise. It establishes a twelve-year monopoly on the printing and sale of the work.</summary>
<keywords>Royal Privilege, Louis XIII, Melchior Mondière, David Laigneau, Alchemy, Book Trade, 17th-century law, Paris</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the text of the "Privilege du Roy" (Royal Privilege), which began on the previous page. It details the penalties for copyright infringement and the requirements for legal deposit before concluding with the official signatures and the date of printing.</meta>

under any disguise or pretext whatsoever without the consent of the said petitioner, upon penalty of a fine <note>original: "amande," an archaic spelling of "amende."</note> of three thousand livres, half to us, the other half to the [aggrieved] party, the confiscation of the said books, and all costs, damages, and interests, provided that the said petitioner shall be bound to deposit three copies—namely, two in our Library <note>The *Bibliothèque du Roi*, the precursor to the National Library of France.</note> and the third for our very dear and faithful Lord **Séguier** <note>Pierre Séguier (1588–1672) was the Chancellor of France and a powerful patron of the arts and sciences who oversaw the regulation of the book trade.</note>, Knight and Chancellor of France—before offering it for sale, upon penalty of forfeiting the Privilege. **THUS WE COMMAND YOU** that you cause the said petitioner, and those acting on his behalf, to enjoy and use the contents of these presents, without allowing him to be disturbed therein; and by placing at the beginning or at the end of the said Book these presents or a brief extract thereof, we will that they be held as verified. For such is our pleasure. Given at Paris the 1st day of September in the year of grace 1636, and of our reign the twenty-seventh.

->By the King in his Council,<-

->Signed **RENOUARD**.<-
